7/8 in

Over a common denominator of 16 the shims are 6/16 + 5/16 + 4/16 = 15/16 in. Adding numerators and denominators separately (9/28 in) is the classic fraction error and gives a stack thinner than the largest shim.

0.7 in

A measured value of 0.046750 in must be reported to three significant digits. Which value should be reported?

Rounded −7.26; truncated −7.26

Rounded −7.26; truncated −7.25

A 31.6% decrease
A 24% increase
A 60% decrease
A 24% decrease
Percent change is (new − original) ÷ original × 100 = (190 − 250) ÷ 250 × 100 = −24%, a 24% decrease. Dividing by the new value (190) instead of the original gives 31.6%.

Defects on line A fell from 40 to 30 per week, and on line B from 400 to 380. A manager says line B improved more because it removed more defects. Which response is correct?
Line B improved more, because removing 20 defects beats removing 10
Both lines improved by the same proportion of their weekly totals
Line A improved more: 25% versus 5% for line B
Line A improved by 33% and line B by about 5% of their new totals
Percent change against each original value puts different-sized bases on equal footing: 10/40 = 25% and 20/400 = 5%. Dividing by the new values (10/30 and 20/380) uses the wrong base.

Setting up 40 + 2.50x = 215 gives 2.50x = 175, so x = 70. Dividing the whole budget by 2.50 (86) ignores the fixed setup fee.

ΔT = ΔL ÷ (α × L)
ΔT = ΔL × α × L
ΔT = (α × L) ÷ ΔL
ΔT = ΔL − (α × L)
Dividing both sides by α × L isolates ΔT. Inverting the fraction, as in (α × L) ÷ ΔL, is the most tempting error and gives the reciprocal of the right answer.

Expanding gives 4x − 8 − 2x − 6 = 0, so 2x = 14 and x = 7. Forgetting to apply the minus sign to the +3 term gives 2x − 2 = 0 and x = 1.

70.9 in²
83.4 in²

Diameter = circumference ÷ π = 47.12 ÷ 3.1416 = 15.00 in. The value 7.50 in is the radius, not the diameter.

A label must wrap once around a can 3.00 in in diameter, with a 0.25 in overlap at the seam. How long must the label be?
Circumference is π × d = π × 3.00 = 9.42 in; adding the 0.25 in overlap gives 9.67 in. Using π × r (4.96 in) covers only half the can.

26 in
38 in
52 in

9.42 ft³

A rectangular parts bin measures 12 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm inside. What volume does it hold in liters?
6 L

Two angles on a fixture are complementary. One measures 32°40′. What does the other measure?
Complementary angles add to 90°: 90°00′ − 32°40′ = 89°60′ − 32°40′ = 57°20′. Forgetting to borrow 60′ from the degrees gives 58°20′, and 147°20′ is the supplement.

Two adjacent angles form a straight line along the edge of a bracket. One angle is 117.5°. What is the other?
Angles on a straight line are supplementary and add to 180°, so 180° − 117.5° = 62.5°. Subtracting 90° (27.5°) treats them as complementary.

A CMM operator must report the diameter and center of a bore in one plane. What is the minimum number of probe points the software needs to calculate a circle?
Two points on opposite sides of the bore
Four points spaced at 90° around the bore
Three points around the bore
Six points evenly spaced around the bore

Three non-collinear points define a unique circle, so three is the mathematical minimum; operators often take more to assess form. Two opposite points give one width only, and many circles pass through them.

Which set gives the minimum number of points needed to define each feature?
Line 2, circle 2, plane 4
Line 3, circle 3, plane 4
Line 1, circle 3, plane 3
Line 2, circle 3, plane 3
Two points define a line, and three non-collinear points define both a circle and a plane. Four points are the minimum for a sphere, not a plane.

Stack height = bar length × sin θ = 5.000 × 0.17365 = 0.86825, which rounds to 0.8682 in (the unrounded sin 10° gives 0.86824 in). Using the cosine (4.9240 in) or the tangent (0.8816 in) applies the wrong ratio to the sine bar triangle.

A 5.000 in sine bar is raised on a 1.2941 in gauge block stack. What angle does the bar make with the surface plate?

A ramp surface 20.0 in long is inclined at 25° to the base. Using cos 25° = 0.9063, what is its horizontal run?
The ramp is the hypotenuse, so run = 20.0 × cos 25° = 18.13 in. The value 8.45 in uses sine and is the vertical rise.

A tapered surface rises at 35° from its base over a horizontal distance of 4.000 in. Using tan 35° = 0.7002, how much does it rise?
Rise is opposite and the 4.000 in run is adjacent, so rise = 4.000 × tan 35° = 2.801 in. Using sine (2.294 in) wrongly treats 4.000 in as the hypotenuse.

By the Pythagorean theorem, √(2.000² + 3.000²) = √13 = 3.606 in. 13.000 in is the sum of the squares before taking the square root.

A right triangle on a weld fixture has a hypotenuse of 10.0 in and one leg of 6.5 in. How long is the other leg?
The missing leg is √(10.0² − 6.5²) = √57.75 = 7.60 in. Adding the squares (11.93 in) solves for a hypotenuse that is already known.

3.2 μin
320 μin
32 μin

875 mm

One inch is exactly 25.4 mm, so 1.2500 × 25.4 = 31.750 mm. Dividing by 25.4 (0.049) converts in the wrong direction.

About 31.5 μin
About 20.3 μin
About 315 μin
About 3.15 μin

3/8 in

Sorted, the data are 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12; with an even count the median is the average of the two middle values, (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6. Taking the middle values without sorting gives (5 + 12) ÷ 2 = 8.5.

An inspector records the defect type on each rejected part: scratch, dent, scratch, burr, scratch, dent. Which measure of central tendency can properly be reported?
The median, which is the dent category
The mean of the numeric defect codes
The mode, which is scratch
The midpoint of the listed categories
Defect types are categories with no numeric order, so only the mode (the most frequent value, scratch) is meaningful. A median requires values that can be ranked, which defect names cannot.

Median of 44 s, as one extreme value inflates the mean
Mean of 56 s, as it is the only measure using all values
Midrange of 80 s, as it is centered between extremes
Mean of 64 s, as it gives the extreme cycle extra weight
The median (44 s) is resistant to the single extreme value, while the mean is pulled up to 336 ÷ 6 = 56 s. The mean uses every value, but that is exactly why one jam distorts it.

Machine B's variance is three times machine A's
Machine B's variance is 0.004 mm² above machine A's
Machine B's variance is nine times machine A's
Machine A has the larger spread of the two machines

Higher speed has been proven to cause the rougher finish
The two variables show a strong negative relationship
The two variables show a strong positive relationship

A bar chart of average coating thickness for each shift

A tally sheet with a row for each defect type

The process is perfectly centered between the limits
The tally sheet has too many cells to show the pattern
Borderline readings recorded as in tolerance
The gauge has too fine a resolution for the parts

A bar chart shows weekly defects of 40 for shift A, 25 for shift B and 60 for shift C. The vertical axis starts at 20 instead of zero. How many times higher is shift C's count than shift B's?
8 times
2.4 times
1.4 times
3.5 times
The actual ratio is 60 ÷ 25 = 2.4. Measuring bar heights above the truncated axis gives (60 − 20) ÷ (25 − 20) = 8, which is why bar charts should start at zero.
std
I.G.4
A supervisor wants to compare last quarter's count of nonconformities for each of six suppliers in a single picture. Which display fits best?
A bar chart with one bar per supplier
A scatter diagram of supplier number against count
A tally sheet of the supplier names alone
A run chart with all six suppliers joined in sequence
Bar charts compare a quantity across separate categories such as suppliers. A scatter diagram needs two numeric variables, and supplier numbers are only labels.
std
I.G.5
Bore diameters follow a normal distribution with a mean of 25.00 mm. About what proportion of bores are larger than 25.00 mm?
A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so half the values lie above it. 68% is the share within ±1 standard deviation, not the share above the mean.
std
I.G.5
For a normal distribution, how do the mean, median and mode compare?
The mean exceeds the median
The mode exceeds the mean
The median is below the mode
They are all equal
Because the normal curve is symmetric with a single peak, the mean, median and mode coincide at the center. A mean above the median indicates right skew, which a normal distribution does not have.
std
I.G.5
Fill weights are normally distributed with a mean of 50.0 g and a standard deviation of 0.2 g. About what percentage of fills fall between 49.6 g and 50.4 g?
About 68%
About 95%
About 99.7%
About 47.5%
49.6 g and 50.4 g are 2 standard deviations either side of the mean, which covers about 95% of a normal distribution. 68% applies to ±1 standard deviation.
std
I.G.5
Shaft lengths are normally distributed with a mean of 10.00 mm and a standard deviation of 0.05 mm. About what percentage exceed 10.10 mm?
About 4.6%
About 47.7%
About 16%
About 2.3%
10.10 mm is 2 standard deviations above the mean; about 95.4% lie within ±2σ, and by symmetry the remaining 4.6% splits evenly, leaving about 2.3% above. 4.6% counts both tails.
std
I.G.5
An inspector builds a histogram of 200 measurements. Which shape is most consistent with a normal distribution?
Two separate peaks of about the same height, side by side
One central peak tapering evenly on both sides
A long tail stretching out toward the right side
Bars of roughly equal height across the whole range
A normal distribution is bell shaped: one peak at the center with frequencies falling off symmetrically. Two peaks usually point to two mixed sources such as two machines or shifts.
std
I.G.5
A process mean drifts upward while its normal shape and spread stay the same. What happens to the bell curve?
It becomes taller and narrower at the center
It develops a long tail on the left side
It slides right with the same width
It becomes wider and flatter around the mean

The mean sets the curve's center and the standard deviation sets its width, so a mean shift moves the whole bell without changing its shape. A wider, flatter curve would mean a larger standard deviation.
std
II.A.1
An inspector reads an inch outside micrometer graduated in 0.001 in. The 0.300 line on the sleeve is visible plus two more minor divisions, and the thimble reads 13. What is the reading?
Each minor sleeve division is 0.025 in, so the reading is 0.300 + 0.050 + 0.013 = 0.363 in. Ignoring the two minor divisions gives 0.313 in, and counting only one gives 0.338 in.
std
II.A.1

Two inspectors measure the same pin with the same micrometer and get readings 0.0004 in apart. One tightens the thimble firmly, the other uses the ratchet stop. What is the most likely cause of the difference?
Thermal growth of the pin from the warmth of the inspectors' hands
A worn spindle thread that only shows up for one of the two operators
Uneven measuring force; the ratchet stop exists to control it
Different lighting that changes how the thimble graduations are read

Variation in measuring force is the classic cause of operator-to-operator differences with micrometers, and the ratchet stop exists to apply a consistent force. Hand heat can matter, but it would affect both inspectors and does not explain one tightening firmly while the other uses the ratchet.
std
II.A.1
An inspector needs to check the depth of a 12 mm deep blind slot with a tolerance of ±0.1 mm. Which use of a standard dial caliper is appropriate?
Depth rod extended, with the beam end square on the top face
Use the outside jaws across the slot and subtract the slot width
Use the step face at the rear of the jaws against the slot floor
Use the inside jaws pressed against the bottom of the slot

A four-way caliper measures depth with the depth rod while the beam end sits flat on the reference face. The step measurement uses the step faces between two shoulders, not a slot floor, and the jaws are for outside and inside sizes.
std
II.A.1
An inspector checks the runout of a shaft turning in centers with a dial indicator. The highest reading is +0.006 mm and the lowest is −0.003 mm. What is the total indicator reading (TIR)?

TIR is the full swing of the indicator: 0.006 − (−0.003) = 0.009 mm. Subtracting the readings as if both were positive gives 0.003 mm, and halving the swing gives 0.0045 mm, which is the radial offset, not TIR.
std
II.A.1
A lever-type dial test indicator is set up with its contact arm at a steep angle to the surface instead of nearly parallel to it. What is the effect on the readings?
The reading is less than the true movement (cosine error)
The readings become erratic only when the indicator is near full travel
The readings are unaffected as long as the indicator is zeroed first
The indicator shows more than the true movement, so parts appear oversize

A test indicator's contact arm swings through an arc, so when the arm sits at an angle to the surface only part of the surface movement turns the arm, and the reading is too small by roughly the cosine of the angle. Zeroing does not remove this error because it scales every change in position, not just the start point. (A plunger indicator tilted to the surface errs the other way, reading high.)
std
II.A.1
Before running a CMM program, the inspector qualifies the probe tip on the machine's reference sphere. What does this step establish?
Effective tip size and offset from the machine axes
The temperature correction for the part material
The part coordinate system based on the drawing datums
The flatness of the CMM table under the fixture

Probe qualification measures the reference sphere to find the effective tip size and offset, which the software needs to compensate every touch. The part coordinate system is set afterward by measuring the part's datum features.
std
II.A.1
An inspector measures a part's length with a steel rule graduated in 1/64 in. To limit parallax error, he should:
Stand the rule on edge and view the graduation square on
Measure from the worn end of the rule so that the zero line is hidden
Read the graduation from a slight angle so that the line looks sharper
Hold the rule flat on its face so the graduations sit well above the part

Parallax comes from viewing a scale at an angle when it is not in contact with the feature, so the eye should be square to the graduation and the edge set on the part. Laying the rule flat on its face raises the graduations away from the edge being measured and makes parallax worse.
std
II.A.1

An inspector must build a 1.3456 in gauge block stack from a set containing 0.1001–0.1009 in (0.0001 steps), 0.101–0.149 in (0.001 steps), 0.050–0.950 in (0.050 steps), and 1, 2, 3 and 4 in blocks. Which stack uses the fewest blocks?

Removing the last digit first with 0.1006 leaves 1.245; 0.145 leaves 1.100; then 0.100 and 1.000 finish the stack, all blocks in the set. Using two 0.050 blocks in place of the 0.100 block adds a block, and the set has no 0.245 or 1.100 block.
std
II.A.1
An inspector wrings several gauge blocks into a stack to set a comparator. What practice keeps the stack accurate?
Use the most blocks possible so each block's error averages out
Clean and wring the blocks, then let the stack stabilize
Hold the stack in a bare hand while setting so it does not slip
Oil the faces generously so that the blocks slide together without wear

Clean, properly wrung faces add almost nothing to the length, and letting the stack stabilize removes heat picked up from handling. Holding the stack in a bare hand warms it and makes it grow, and adding blocks adds wringing films and error rather than averaging it out.
std
II.A.1
An inspector needs to check the inside of a cast hydraulic passage for loose sand and porosity without cutting the part. Which instrument is most suitable?
A dial bore gauge set with a master ring
A steel rule and a hand-held magnifier
A borescope fed in through an existing port
A telescoping gauge read with a micrometer

A borescope carries an image out of a passage the eye cannot reach, so it suits visual checks for debris or porosity inside a part. A dial bore gauge measures diameter but shows nothing about the condition of the surface.
std
II.A.1
A steel part 100 mm long is measured at 30 °C. The coefficient of expansion is 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, and the reference temperature is 20 °C. About how much longer is the part than it would be at 20 °C?
Growth = 100 × 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ × (30 − 20) = 0.0115 mm. Using 1 °C instead of the 10 °C difference gives 0.00115 mm, and using the full 30 °C gives 0.0345 mm.
std
II.A.1
A precision part has just come off a machine and feels warm. Before final measurement with gauges at the 20 °C reference, what should the inspector do?
Measure it right away because the gauge is warming at the same rate
Measure it right away and add the tolerance band to cover the heat
Cool it quickly with compressed air and measure while it is still damp
Let it soak until a probe shows it near gauge temperature

A temperature probe confirms when the part has stabilized near the gauge and room temperature, which removes most thermal error. Forced cooling leaves the part uneven in temperature, and the gauge and part do not change temperature at the same rate.
std
II.A.2
An inspector checks a tapped hole with a thread plug gauge. The GO member turns in for the full thread length and the NOT GO member will not enter. What should she conclude?
The result is unclear and a micrometer reading is needed
The thread is oversize and must be rejected
The thread is within the gauged limits and is accepted
The thread is undersize and must be retapped

A thread that accepts the GO member fully and rejects the NOT GO member is within the limits the gauge represents. An undersize thread would stop the GO member, and an oversize thread would let the NOT GO member enter.
std
II.A.2
A gauge has a GO diameter and a NOT GO diameter on the same end, one behind the other. What is this gauge called, and how is it used?
A double-end plug; each end is used in a separate operation on the hole
A step pin; the larger step should enter and the smaller should not
A progressive plug; the first step enters, the second must not
A taper plug; it is pushed in until it stops and the depth is read
A progressive gauge places the GO and NOT GO sections in sequence, so one insertion checks both limits. A double-end plug puts the GO and NOT GO on opposite ends, which needs two separate insertions.
std
II.A.2
A machinist turns a shaft and asks inspection to check it with fixed-limit gauges. Which gauge type is meant for this external diameter?
A flush pin gauge
A progressive thread plug gauge
A GO and NOT GO ring gauge pair
A GO and NOT GO pin gauge pair
Ring gauges fit over external cylindrical features, the GO ring passing over the shaft and the NOT GO ring not passing. Pin gauges are plugs that check holes, not shafts.
std
II.A.2
An inspector checks the depth of a counterbore with a flush pin gauge. The end of the pin is below the high step on the gauge body but above the low step. What does this show?
The depth is within the limits, so it is accepted
The depth is past the maximum and the feature is rejected
The gauge is out of adjustment and must be reset
The depth is below the minimum and the feature is rejected

On a flush pin gauge, the two steps on the body mark the limits, so a pin end that falls between them means the feature is within tolerance. A reading outside the steps, not between them, would indicate a reject.
std
II.A.2
An inspector uses pin gauges to check a hole specified as 6.00 to 6.05 mm. The 6.00 pin enters and the 6.05 pin does not. What can she correctly report?
The hole size is exactly 6.025 mm, the midpoint between the pins
The hole is round within 0.05 mm along its whole length
The hole is within the limits to the depth the pins reached
The hole is oversize because the smaller pin entered
Pin gauges give an attribute result: the hole is at least as large as the entering pin and smaller than the pin that will not enter. They do not give an actual size or prove roundness along the hole.
std
II.A.2
An inspector holds a radius gauge leaf against a fillet and sees light showing at both ends of the contact but none in the middle. What does this indicate?
The fillet radius matches the radius of that leaf exactly
The fillet radius is larger than the radius of that leaf
The leaf is a concave type and cannot be used on a fillet
The fillet radius is smaller than the radius of that leaf
A convex leaf in a larger concave fillet touches only at the middle, leaving gaps at the ends. If the fillet were smaller than the leaf, the leaf would touch at the ends and show light in the middle.
std
II.A.3
An inspector must measure a 0.250 in hole that is too small for a telescoping gauge. Which tool and method are appropriate?
A small-hole gauge set to a light drag, read with a micrometer
A spring caliper set to the hole and read on a steel rule to 0.001 in
A small-hole gauge read directly from the scale on its knurled knob
A telescoping gauge locked and read directly from its handle markings

Small-hole gauges cover holes too small for telescoping gauges; the split ball is set to a light drag and then measured over the ball with a micrometer. The gauge has no scale of its own, so it cannot be read directly.
std
II.A.3
When using a telescoping gauge in a bore, the inspector locks it while rocking it through the bore. Why is the gauge rocked?
So the plungers settle on the true diameter, not a chord
So the lock does not slip when the gauge is withdrawn
So the gauge reaches the temperature of the bore first
So the plungers wear evenly over the whole life of the gauge
Rocking the gauge through center lets the plungers close to the largest dimension, the true diameter, before locking. A gauge locked off center measures a chord, which is shorter than the diameter.
std
II.A.3
An inspector compares a telescoping gauge reading with a bore gauge reading and finds the telescoping gauge consistently small. Which technique error most likely explains this?
Using a telescoping gauge whose range covers the bore diameter
Letting the gauge settle to room temperature before reading it
Measuring the telescoping gauge with a micrometer of finer resolution
Excess micrometer force pushing the plungers in
Too much micrometer force compresses the plungers of the locked gauge and makes the transfer read small. A finer micrometer and a gauge of the right range are good practice, not error sources.
std
II.A.3
A spring caliper is used to pick up an outside diameter on a rough casting. How is the size then determined?
By comparing the caliper to a GO and NOT GO ring set
By reading the scale engraved on the caliper's spring
By measuring its setting with a rule or micrometer
By reading the dial mounted at the caliper's pivot

A spring caliper has no scale; it holds a setting that is then measured with a rule or micrometer, which is why it is called a transfer gauge. Engraved scales and dials belong to direct-reading instruments.
std
II.A.4

An inch vernier caliper has a main scale graduated in 0.025 in and a 25-division vernier. The vernier zero is past the 1.400 in mark plus three 0.025 in divisions, and the 11th vernier line coincides with a main scale line. What is the reading?
The reading is the main scale value 1.475 plus 11 × 0.001 = 1.486 in. Dropping the three 0.025 divisions past 1.400 gives 1.411 in, and ignoring the vernier gives 1.475 in.
std
II.A.4
A metric vernier caliper reads to 0.02 mm. The vernier zero is just past 23 mm on the main scale, and the 17th vernier division lines up with a main scale line. What is the reading?
Each vernier division is worth 0.02 mm, so the reading is 23 + 17 × 0.02 = 23.34 mm. Reading the division count as hundredths gives 23.17 mm.
std
II.A.4
At the start of a shift, a dial caliper's needle points to 0.002 in with the jaws clean and fully closed. What should the inspector do first?
Zero the bezel, then verify on a gauge block
Subtract 0.002 in from every reading taken later that shift
Add 0.002 in to every reading and record the correction
Tag the caliper out of calibration and send it to the lab

A dial caliper's bezel is meant to be zeroed with the jaws closed, and a check on a gauge block confirms the caliper reads correctly across its range. Carrying a mental correction through the shift invites mistakes and does not confirm the caliper is sound.
std
II.A.4
A digital caliper displays to 0.01 mm. A new inspector says this proves the caliper is accurate to 0.01 mm. Which reply is correct?
Accuracy is double the resolution, so this caliper is accurate to 0.02 mm
Accuracy is the resolution only after the zero button has been pressed
The display can only show values that the caliper has the accuracy to measure correctly
Display resolution is not accuracy; accuracy comes from calibration against standards

Resolution is the smallest change the display shows, while accuracy is how close the reading is to the true value, which only calibration establishes. Rules of thumb like doubling the resolution have no basis and do not replace calibration data.
std
II.B.1
Which instrument displays how a voltage signal changes over time as a waveform?
A digital multimeter
A data logger
An oscilloscope
A load cell
An oscilloscope plots voltage against time, showing the shape, frequency and amplitude of a signal. A multimeter gives a single numeric value, such as an RMS voltage, and does not show the waveform.
std
II.B.1
An inspector needs to measure the current drawn by a small motor using a digital multimeter. How must the meter be connected?
In parallel across the motor terminals, like a voltage reading
Across the supply with the motor disconnected from the circuit
In series with the motor, so the current flows through the meter
Across the motor with the meter switched to its resistance range
Current is measured by placing the meter in the circuit path so the current passes through it. Connecting an ammeter in parallel, as for voltage, can short the circuit and blow the meter's fuse.
std
II.B.1
A test technician uses a multimeter to check whether a heater element has an open circuit. Which setting and condition are correct?
Voltage range, with the element powered and in operation
Resistance range, with power removed from the element
Resistance range, with the element powered and in operation
Current range, with the element powered and in operation

Resistance is measured with power off, because the meter supplies its own small test current; an open circuit reads as infinite resistance. Measuring resistance on a live circuit gives false readings and can damage the meter.
std
II.B.2
A line uses a camera, controlled lighting and image-processing software to check every label for presence and position. What kind of gauging is this?
Ultrasonic gauging
Pneumatic gauging
Machine vision
Laser micrometry

Machine vision captures images and uses software to judge features such as presence, position and size. Laser micrometers measure a dimension from a shadowed beam and do not inspect labels in this way.
std
II.B.2
A tank fabricator needs to measure remaining wall thickness on a pipe that can be reached from the outside only. Which automatic gauging method fits?
Machine vision imaging of the outer surface
A pneumatic probe set with a master ring
Laser profile scanning of the whole outer surface
Ultrasonic thickness gauging with a couplant
Ultrasonic gauging times sound reflected from the inner wall, so thickness can be measured from one side. Imaging or laser scanning of the outside surface cannot see the inner wall.
std
II.B.2
A supplier needs to find internal voids in aluminum castings and confirm internal passages are present without cutting the parts. Which automatic gauging method is best suited?
Pneumatic gauging of the bores
X-ray (radiographic or CT) inspection
Laser triangulation of the outer surface
Machine vision with ring lighting
X-rays pass through the part and show differences in density, revealing voids and hidden passages. Laser and vision systems see only external surfaces.
std
II.B.2
A wire mill wants continuous, noncontact diameter measurement of wire running at high speed. Which automatic gauging method is most suitable?
A scanning laser micrometer
An ultrasonic thickness gauge
An X-ray cabinet beside the line
A flush pin gauge on the line
A scanning laser micrometer measures the shadow the wire casts in a moving beam, without contact and at high speed. Ultrasonic gauges need a couplant and contact, which does not suit a moving wire.
std
II.B.3
How does a pneumatic (air) plug gauge sense the diameter of a bore?
It senses the time for sound to echo back from the bore wall
It senses changes in back pressure or air flow at jets near the bore wall
It senses the light that the jets reflect back from the bore wall
It senses the travel of spring-loaded contact points against the bore wall
Air escaping from the jets is restricted more as the wall gets closer, so pressure or flow changes with the bore size. The jets do not touch the wall, which is why air gauging is noncontact.
std
II.B.3
An inspector sets up an air plug gauge on a column. What does he use to set the gauge?
Minimum and maximum master rings
A GO and NOT GO pin gauge pair
The first production part of the lot
A single gauge block at the nominal size
Air gauges are comparators, so they are set with masters near the limits to set zero and magnification. A first production part is not a known standard and cannot set the gauge.
std
II.B.3
Which pneumatic gauging component measures an external diameter such as a pin or shaft?
An air jet depth probe
An air plug gauge
An air ring gauge
An air plug with a single jet
An air ring surrounds the part with jets facing inward, so it measures external diameters. An air plug goes into a bore and measures internal diameters.
std
II.B.4
An assembler uses a click-type torque wrench. Which practice supports accurate torque?
Hold the wrench near the head for better control of the pull
Use the wrench to break loose fasteners before final torque
Pull steadily on the handle grip until the click, then stop
Keep pulling after the click to be sure the fastener is tight

The wrench is set for force on the handle grip, and pulling past the click overshoots the setting. Holding near the head shortens the lever arm and changes the torque applied, and breaking loose fasteners can damage the mechanism.
std
II.B.4
A click-type torque wrench is put away at the end of the shift. What is recommended?
Set it to its highest setting to keep the spring stretched
Leave it at the last setting so the next user can start at once
Lubricate the internal spring and store it unlocked
Set it back to the lowest marked setting before storage
Storing a click wrench at its lowest setting relieves the spring, which helps it hold calibration. Leaving it at a high setting keeps the spring compressed and can change its rate over time.
std
II.B.4
What does a strain-gauge load cell do?
It converts an applied force into a visual color change
It converts an applied force into an electrical signal
It converts a part's temperature into a force
It converts an applied torque into an air pressure
A load cell's strain gauges change resistance as the cell deforms under load, giving an electrical signal proportional to force. It is used in tensile testers, force gauges and scales.
std
II.B.5
A lab needs a continuous paper record of temperature in a heat-treat oven over each shift. Which instrument provides this?
A dial thermometer
A chart recorder
A digital multimeter
A handheld infrared gun
A chart recorder draws a continuous trace of the measured value on a chart moving with time. A dial thermometer or handheld gun shows only the current reading and keeps no record.
std
II.B.5
A data logger records cold-room temperature every 30 minutes. A door is left open for 10 minutes between two readings. What risk does this present?
The logger will fail, because loggers stop recording during a sudden change
The event may fall between samples and go unrecorded
The logger will store the event and show it at its next scheduled download
The logger will average the event across the whole 30-minute interval
A data logger records only at its sampling times, so a short event between samples can go unseen. Choosing an interval suited to the events that matter is part of setting up a logger.
std
II.B.5
A metrology lab wants temperature and humidity records stored electronically so they can be downloaded and charted later. Which device suits this best?
A bimetal thermometer
A chart recorder
A sling psychrometer
A data logger
A data logger stores time-stamped readings in memory for download and analysis. A chart recorder keeps a paper trace, and a sling psychrometer gives a spot reading of humidity.
std
II.C.1
A shaft is toleranced 25.00 ± 0.05 mm. Under the 10:1 rule, what is the coarsest gauge resolution the inspector may use?
The total tolerance is 0.10 mm, and one tenth of that is 0.01 mm. Taking one tenth of the ±0.05 mm half-tolerance gives 0.005 mm, which is finer than needed.
std
II.C.1
An inspection micrometer has an accuracy of 0.0005 in. Under the 10:1 rule, what is the coarsest accuracy the gauge blocks used to calibrate it may have?

The standard should be ten times better than the instrument it calibrates: 0.0005 / 10 = 0.00005 in. Using the same 0.0005 in value gives no margin, and 0.005 in is ten times worse rather than better.
std
II.C.1
A hole tolerance is 0.010 in total. The only available gauge resolves 0.002 in. What does the 10:1 rule indicate?
The gauge is not adequate; 0.001 in or finer is needed
The gauge is adequate if the tolerance is widened to 0.012 in
The gauge is adequate if each reading is repeated three times
The gauge is adequate because 0.002 in is smaller than 0.010 in

One tenth of 0.010 in is 0.001 in, so a gauge that resolves only 0.002 in uses a fifth of the tolerance. Being smaller than the tolerance is not enough, and an inspector cannot widen a tolerance to fit a gauge.
std
II.C.1
What is the purpose of the 10:1 rule applied between calibration standards and inspection gauges?
To ensure inspection gauges are calibrated ten times more often than standards
To set calibration intervals at one tenth of the gauge's expected life
To keep the standard's error small relative to the gauge being calibrated
To allow inspection gauges ten times the error stated by the manufacturer

A standard that is ten times better than the gauge contributes little error to the calibration, so the gauge's calibrated value can be trusted. The rule concerns accuracy ratios, not how often items are calibrated.
std
II.C.2
An inspector must check the pitch diameter of an external thread. Which gauge is best matched to this characteristic?
A radius gauge on the thread roots
An outside micrometer on the crests
Thread wires used with a micrometer
A vernier caliper on the major diameter
The three-wire method contacts the thread flanks, so the measurement relates to pitch diameter. A micrometer on the crests measures major diameter, which is a different characteristic.
std
II.C.2
Two features on a drawing are toleranced ±0.5 mm and ±0.005 mm. Which gauge plan suits them?
A steel rule for the ±0.005 mm feature and a caliper for the ±0.5 mm one
A micrometer for the ±0.5 mm feature and a caliper for the ±0.005 mm one
A caliper for both features, because the caliper covers both sizes
A caliper for ±0.5 mm and a micrometer or comparator for ±0.005 mm
Gauge choice follows the tolerance: a wide tolerance allows a quick general instrument, while a tight one needs a finer instrument. A caliper does not have the accuracy to judge a ±0.005 mm feature.
std
II.C.2

Two micrometers resolve 0.001 mm. One has a calibration certificate showing errors up to 0.004 mm across its range, and the other shows errors up to 0.001 mm. For a tight-tolerance part, how should the inspector choose?
Choose either one, because both resolve 0.001 mm and so measure equally well
Choose the one most recently used, since it will already be at room temperature
Choose the one with larger error, since it was found and corrected in calibration
Choose the one with the smaller calibrated error
Accuracy is shown by the calibration errors, not by how finely the instrument displays, so the 0.001 mm instrument is the better choice. Equal resolution does not mean equal accuracy.
std
II.C.2
A gauge is needed for receiving inspection on a dusty, unheated loading dock. Which consideration should weigh most in choosing the gauge?
Whether the gauge has the finest resolution available from the supplier
Whether it stays accurate in that area's dirt and temperature swings
Whether the gauge is the same brand as the gauges in the lab
Whether the gauge has the newest software for storing measurements

The use environment affects gauge accuracy, so a gauge must be robust to the dirt and temperature where it will be used, or the work must move. Finer resolution means nothing if the environment ruins the readings.
std
II.C.2
A characteristic has a total tolerance of 0.02 mm. Which instrument resolution is suitable?
0.1 mm
Resolution should be about one tenth of the tolerance or better, so 0.002 mm or finer is needed and 0.001 mm qualifies. A 0.01 mm resolution would split the tolerance into only two steps.
std
II.C.2
A gauge passed calibration, but a Gage R&R study shows its variation consumes 45% of the part tolerance. What does this mean for selecting it for the job?
It is not capable, so its calibration certificate must be voided
It is capable, provided the readings are averaged across shifts
It is capable, because passing calibration proves it suits the job
It is not capable for this tolerance, even though it is calibrated

Calibration shows the gauge is accurate against standards, while a Gage R&R shows whether its variation in use is small relative to the tolerance; 45% is generally unacceptable. The calibration itself is still valid; the gauge is simply unsuited to this tolerance.
std
II.C.2
An inspector measures a pin diameter by reading the value straight off an outside micrometer. What type of measurement is this?
Direct measurement
Differential measurement
Transfer measurement
Comparative measurement

In a direct measurement the instrument itself shows the size of the feature. Differential or comparative measurement reads only the deviation from a master, and transfer measurement uses a second instrument to read the size picked up.
std
II.C.2
An inspector zeros a dial indicator on a gauge block stack of the nominal height, then reads each part's deviation from that zero. What type of measurement is this?
Attribute measurement
Comparative measurement
Direct reading measurement
Transfer gauge measurement
Setting the indicator on a master and reading only deviations from it is differential, or comparative, measurement. It is not direct, because the indicator does not show the full size of the part.
std
II.C.2
Why is differential measurement against a master often chosen for tight tolerances?
The method works without cleaning the part or the master block
Only the small deviation is read, so high magnification can be used
The indicator needs no master, so standard errors are removed entirely
The method makes the reading independent of temperature changes

Because only the small difference from the master is read, a high-magnification indicator can be used, and many instrument errors cancel. The method still depends on the master's accuracy and on cleanliness and temperature.
std
II.C.2
An inspector must measure a groove diameter inside a bore where no direct-reading instrument fits. Which measurement approach is appropriate?
Direct measurement with a steel rule inserted into the bore
Differential measurement with a height gauge on the bore face
Direct measurement with an outside micrometer across the bore mouth
Transfer measurement with a telescoping gauge read on a micrometer

When the feature cannot be reached by a reading instrument, a transfer gauge picks up the size and a micrometer measures the gauge. A micrometer across the bore mouth would measure the mouth, not the groove inside.
std
II.C.3
Steel gauge blocks are being put away after use in a humid area. What should the inspector do?
Leave them wrung together in a stack so their faces are protected
Store them loose in a drawer with the other bench tools
Clean them, apply a thin rust preventive film, and case them
Rinse them with water, let them air dry, and leave them wrung together
Fingerprints and moisture cause corrosion, so blocks are cleaned, lightly protected and stored in their case. Leaving blocks wrung together can cause the faces to corrode or bond.
std
II.C.3
How should an outside micrometer be stored when not in use?
With the anvil and spindle closed tightly to protect the faces
With the spindle lock on and the faces under light pressure
Hanging from its frame on a hook near the machine
With the anvil and spindle faces slightly apart, in its case

Leaving a small gap prevents stress on the frame from temperature changes and lets air reach the faces so they do not corrode. Storing the faces closed under pressure can strain the frame and hold moisture between the faces.
std
II.C.3
Before checking a part, an inspector notices a light film of oil and chips on the measuring faces of a caliper. What should he do?
Blow the faces off with shop air and measure immediately
Measure the part anyway and add the film thickness to the reading
Use an abrasive pad to remove the film from the faces
Wipe with a lint-free cloth and cleaner, then check zero

Clean, lint-free wiping removes debris without damaging the faces, and a zero check confirms the result. Shop air can drive grit into the slide and carries moisture and oil, and abrasives damage measuring faces.
std
II.C.3
During a measurement, an inspector holds a long gauge block in her bare hand for several minutes. What is the main concern?
Hand heat makes it grow; gloves or tongs should be used
Skin oils will change the block's grade until it is recalibrated
The block will become magnetized from being handled by hand
The block's surface finish will be worn by the contact with skin
Hand heat expands steel blocks enough to matter for precision work, which is why insulating grips or gloves are used. Skin oil is a corrosion concern but does not change the block's grade.
std
II.C.4
A plant has two bench gauges checking the same feature, and operators get different results depending on which one they use. What is the best way to establish correlation?
Measure the same parts on both gauges and compare each pair
Measure one part on each gauge and adjust the higher one to match
Recalibrate both gauges and assume they now agree on parts
Measure different parts on each gauge and compare the two averages

Measuring the same parts on both gauges isolates the gauge difference from part variation, and paired differences show any bias. Comparing averages from different parts mixes part variation into the comparison.
std
II.C.4
Five parts are measured on gauge A and gauge B. The differences (A − B) are +0.002, +0.003, +0.001, +0.002 and +0.002 mm. What is the average bias of gauge A relative to gauge B?

The average difference is (0.002 + 0.003 + 0.001 + 0.002 + 0.002) / 5 = 0.010 / 5 = +0.002 mm. The sum, 0.010 mm, is not the average, and the smallest or largest single difference does not represent the bias.
std
II.C.4
A plant replaces hand micrometer checks with an automated laser gauge. What should be done before the laser results are accepted in place of the micrometer results?
Check that the laser gauge's resolution is finer than the micrometer's
Run the laser gauge for a week and review its readings for any outliers
Accept the laser gauge because automated systems remove operator error
Measure the same parts both ways and confirm they agree

A manual-to-automated correlation study measures the same parts by both methods to find and resolve any systematic difference. Removing operator error does not prove the new method measures the same thing the old one did.
std
II.C.4
A correlation study shows that a vision system reads hole diameters 0.015 mm larger than a CMM, consistently across the range. What is the most appropriate next step?
Ignore the difference because both systems are calibrated
Discard the CMM results because the vision system checks more parts
Average the two systems' readings for each hole from now on
Find the cause, such as edge detection versus probe contact

A consistent offset points to a method difference that must be understood before deciding how to correct or compensate. Calibration of each system alone does not guarantee they measure the feature the same way.
std
II.D.1

Using a height gauge with an indicator on a surface plate, an inspector reads 1.240 in at the bottom edge of a cross hole and 1.740 in at the top edge. What is the height of the hole center above the plate?
The center is midway between the two edges: (1.240 + 1.740) / 2 = 1.490 in. The difference, 0.500 in, is the hole diameter, and half of it, 0.250 in, is the radius.
std
II.D.1
An inspector uses a height gauge on a surface plate. What serves as the reference datum for the measurements?
The highest point found on the part fixture
The scriber tip after it has been sharpened
The surface plate under the gauge and the part
The top surface of the part that is being measured
The plate is the datum plane that both the height gauge base and the part sit on, so heights are measured from it. The part's own top surface is a measured feature, not the reference.
std
II.D.1
An inspector needs to check the runout of a shaft and has no centers available. How can V-blocks be used?
Set the V-block on the shaft and read the gap with feeler gauges
Clamp the shaft upright in one V-block and read its height with a scriber
Rotate it in matched V-blocks under an indicator
Rest the shaft across two V-blocks of different sizes and read the angle
Matched V-blocks support a cylinder on the same axis height so it can be rotated under an indicator. Using unmatched blocks would tilt the shaft and add error.
std
II.D.1
A shaft with three-lobed out-of-roundness is checked in a V-block with an indicator. What should the inspector be aware of?
The V-block setup cannot detect any out-of-roundness at all
The V-block setup measures roundness exactly like a roundness tester
The reading varies with V angle and lobe count
The V-block setup will show twice the true form error, whatever the angle

In a V-block, the part's own lobes shift it as it turns, so the reading depends on the number of lobes and the V angle and may not equal the true error. A roundness tester measures against a precise axis and avoids this effect.
std
II.D.1
To check the parallelism of a part's top face to its bottom face on a surface plate, an inspector should:
Hold an indicator by hand and slide it along the top face
Bottom face on the plate; sweep the top with a stand indicator
Rest the top face on the plate and read heights with a steel rule
Measure thickness at one point with a micrometer and compare it to print

With the bottom face on the plate as datum, sweeping the top face with a stand-mounted indicator shows the full height variation. A single micrometer reading tells nothing about variation across the face.
std
II.D.1
Which practice protects the accuracy of a granite surface plate?
Do all measurements in the center to keep the edges sharp
Clean it, cover it when idle, and spread work across it
Clean it with water only and leave it uncovered to dry
Use it as a work bench for light assembly when it is idle
Dirt and concentrated use wear a plate unevenly, so regular cleaning, covering and spreading the work help keep it flat. Using it as a bench and working only in the center both cause local wear.
std
II.D.1
During calibration of a surface plate, the lab measures both overall flatness and repeat readings. What do repeat readings detect?
The average height of the plate above the floor
Local wear within small areas of the plate
The squareness of the plate's edges to its face
The hardness of the granite at the surface

Overall flatness checks the whole surface, while repeat-reading gauges check small local areas for wear that the overall survey may miss. Hardness and edge squareness are not part of a plate's flatness calibration.
std
II.D.1
A surface plate's calibration shows it is out of its flatness grade. What is the usual corrective action?
Polish it with fine sandpaper during the next shift
Have it lapped to restore flatness and then recalibrated
Downgrade the tolerance on the parts measured on it
Shim the plate's legs until its surface reads level again
Lapping removes material in a controlled way to restore flatness, and recalibration confirms the grade. Leveling the plate by shimming changes its tilt, not its flatness.
std
II.D.2
A 5 in sine bar is to be set at 20°. What gauge block height is needed under the raised roll? (sin 20° = 0.34202)
Height = length × sin θ = 5 × 0.34202 = 1.7101 in. Using cosine instead gives 4.6985 in, and 1.8199 in comes from using tangent.
std
II.D.2
A 5 in sine bar rests on a 2.1131 in gauge block stack. What angle does it set?
sin θ = 2.1131 / 5 = 0.42262, which is sin 25°. Taking the complementary angle gives 65°, using arctangent gives 22.9°, and 0.42 is the sine ratio itself, not an angle.
std
II.D.2
Why are sine bars generally not used for angles much above 45°?
The sine bar rolls lift off the plate above an angle of 45°
Block height errors cause larger angle errors at steep angles
The sine function stops rising above 45°, so readings repeat
The gauge blocks needed above 45° are not made in standard sets
As the angle increases, the sine changes more slowly, so a given height error produces a larger angle error. Standard block sets can build the needed heights, and the sine keeps rising to 90°.
std
II.D.2
An inspector uses a universal bevel protractor with a vernier to check a chamfer. What resolution can such a protractor typically give?
5 minutes of arc
30 seconds of arc
1 degree
1 second of arc

A vernier bevel protractor normally reads to 5 minutes. Resolving 1 second needs methods such as angle blocks or an autocollimator, and 1 degree is the resolution of a plain protractor without a vernier.
std
II.D.2
An inspector has angle blocks of 1°, 3°, 5°, 15°, 30° and 45° and needs to set 12°. What is the best way?
Wring the 30° block with the 15° block reversed and halve it
Wring the 15° block with the 3° block reversed so the angles subtract
Wring the 15° block with the 1° block and rotate it 3°
Wring the 5°, 3°, 3° and 1° blocks together so the angles add
Angle blocks can be reversed so their angles subtract: 15° − 3° = 12° with two blocks. Adding 5 + 3 + 3 + 1 needs a second 3° block that the set does not contain, and 30° − 15° gives 15°, not 12°.
std
II.E.1
A spring scale and an equal-arm balance are both moved to a site where gravity is slightly weaker. Which statement is correct?
The spring scale reading changes, but the balance still compares mass correctly
Neither reading changes, because both instruments measure mass directly
Both readings change by the same amount, so neither is affected relative to the other
The balance reading changes, but the spring scale still reads mass correctly

A spring scale measures the force of gravity on the load, so its reading changes with local gravity. A balance compares the load with reference masses that are affected by gravity equally, so it measures mass.
std
II.E.1
A lab technician checks an analytical balance with a certified reference weight. Which handling practice is correct?
Blow on the weight before use to remove any dust from its surface
Lift the weight by hand so its temperature matches the operator's
Clean the weight with an abrasive cloth if it looks dull
Handle it with tweezers or gloves to keep oils and moisture off
Skin oils and moisture add mass and cause corrosion, so reference weights are handled with tweezers or gloves. Abrasive cleaning removes material and changes the mass.
std
II.E.1
A container weighs 0.380 kg empty. Filled, it reads 2.450 kg on a scale. What is the net mass of the contents?
Net = gross − tare = 2.450 − 0.380 = 2.070 kg. Adding the tare gives 2.830 kg, and the gross reading includes the container.
std
II.E.1
Readings on a precision electronic balance drift and vary from reading to reading. Which condition is the most likely cause?
A draft, vibration, or the balance not being level
Using a tare before placing the sample on the pan
The balance's display set to show too many decimal places
Calibrating the balance with its internal weight function

Precision balances are sensitive to drafts, vibration and leveling, which is why draft shields, stable tables and a level bubble are used. Taring and internal calibration are normal practice and do not cause drift.
std
II.E.2
When checking a turned surface with a stylus profilometer, in which direction should the stylus traverse?
At 45° to the lay, to average the two directions
Along the lay, in the direction of the tool marks
Across the lay, at right angles to the tool marks
In any direction, because Ra does not depend on lay

Traversing across the lay captures the peaks and valleys left by the tool, which is the roughness the specification usually controls. Traversing along the lay misses most of that texture and gives a low reading.
std
II.E.2
A stylus profilometer reports Ra for a surface. What does Ra represent?
The largest single peak height above the mean line
The height from the highest peak to the lowest valley in the sample
The arithmetic average of absolute deviations from the mean line
The spacing between peaks along the evaluation length
Ra is the arithmetic mean of the absolute deviations of the profile from the mean line. Peak-to-valley height is a different parameter, such as Rt or Rz.
std
II.E.2
A soft polymer lens surface must have its roughness measured without marking it. Which instrument is best suited?
An optical (noncontact) profilometer
A dial indicator swept across the surface
A diamond-tip stylus profilometer
A comparison specimen and a fingernail
An optical profilometer measures the surface with light, so it cannot scratch a soft surface. A stylus can mark soft materials, and a comparison specimen gives only a rough tactile judgment.
std
II.E.3
How does a mechanical comparator measure a part?
It reads the part's full size directly from a long engraved scale
It senses the air flow escaping between jets and the part
It magnifies small differences from a master by levers
It projects an enlarged image of the part onto a screen

A mechanical comparator is set to a master, then its lever or gear system magnifies small deviations so they can be read. Projecting an image describes an optical comparator, and sensing air flow describes pneumatic gauging.
std
II.E.3
Why does a two-point micrometer check often fail to detect odd-lobed (for example, three-lobed) out-of-roundness?
The diameter is nearly constant across every pair of opposite points
The lobes only appear when the part is rotated at speed
The micrometer's anvil flattens the lobes during the check
The micrometer's resolution is too coarse to show lobing of that small size

An odd-lobed part has a nearly constant width, so two-point checks show little change even though the part is not round. A roundness tester, which measures radial deviations from an axis, reveals the lobes.
std
II.E.3
On a roundness tester, what role does the precision spindle play?
It drives the stylus across the surface to measure the roughness profile
It provides an accurate axis of rotation that serves as the reference
It reads the part's diameter by counting turns of the spindle screw
It holds the part still while the operator rotates the probe by hand

A roundness tester measures radial changes relative to the spindle's axis, so the spindle's own error must be far smaller than the form error being measured. It is not a screw for reading diameter or a roughness drive.
std
II.E.3
A profile tracer is used on a turbine blade edge. What does it produce?
A color image of the blade surface for visual review
A single reading of the blade's thickness at its midpoint
A reading of the blade's hardness along the edge
A contour trace to compare with the nominal profile

A profile (contour) tracer moves a stylus along the surface and records its shape, which is then compared with the nominal contour or tolerance zone. A single thickness reading says nothing about the contour.
std
II.E.4
On an optical comparator set at 20X, a feature's image measures 50.0 mm on the screen. What is the actual feature size?
Actual size = image size / magnification = 50.0 / 20 = 2.50 mm. Multiplying instead gives 1000 mm, and dividing by 2 instead of 20 gives 25.0 mm.
std
II.E.4
An inspector checks a stamped profile on an optical comparator using an overlay chart. Which condition must be met?
The overlay chart must be drawn at the same magnification as the lens in use
The overlay chart must be drawn at twice the lens magnification for clarity
The overlay chart can be drawn at any scale, because the software rescales it
The overlay chart must be drawn at full size and placed under the part
The chart is a magnified drawing of the tolerance zone, so it must match the lens magnification to compare correctly with the shadow. A full-size chart could not be compared with an enlarged image.
std
II.E.4
A measuring microscope has a 10X eyepiece and a 40X objective. What is the total magnification?
4X
Total magnification is the product of the eyepiece and objective: 10 × 40 = 400X. Adding them gives 50X.
std
II.E.4
An inspector uses a toolmaker's microscope to check the spacing of fine lines on a part. Compared with low magnification, what happens when she switches to a higher-power objective?
The field of view and depth of focus both become smaller
The field of view and depth of focus both become larger
The field of view grows while depth of focus stays the same
The working distance increases while the field stays the same
Higher magnification shows a smaller area and has a shallower depth of focus, so focusing becomes more critical. Field of view does not grow with magnification; it shrinks.
std
II.E.5
A vision camera covers a 50 mm field of view with 2000 pixels across. The feature tolerance is ±0.1 mm. Does the pixel size meet the 10:1 rule?
Yes; each pixel is 0.0025 mm, well within the 0.02 mm that is needed
Yes; each pixel is 0.025 mm, finer than the 0.1 mm limit
No; each pixel is 0.25 mm, coarser than the 0.1 mm limit
No; each pixel is 0.025 mm, coarser than the 0.02 mm needed

Pixel size = 50 / 2000 = 0.025 mm, while one tenth of the 0.2 mm total tolerance is 0.02 mm, so it falls short. Comparing pixel size with the ±0.1 mm limit rather than one tenth of the total tolerance wrongly suggests it is adequate.
std
II.E.5
A blue light 3D scanner produces a color map comparing a scanned casting with its CAD model. What does the scanner fundamentally capture?
A set of discrete touch points at preset probe locations
A silhouette of the part outline projected at fixed scale
A dense cloud of surface points from projected patterns
A cross-section image showing internal density changes

Structured light scanners project fringe patterns and calculate millions of surface points, which software compares with CAD. Discrete touch points describe a contact CMM, and density images describe X-ray.
std
II.E.5
Why is blue light often chosen over white light for structured light scanners in shop areas?
It can pass through the part to show internal features
It removes the need to calibrate the scanner before use
Its narrow light band is less disturbed by ambient lighting
It makes shiny and dark surfaces scan exactly like matte ones

Narrow-band blue light can be filtered from ambient light, which improves data quality in lit areas. Shiny and dark surfaces remain a challenge for any light-based scanner, and calibration is still needed.
std
II.E.5
An inspector uses a handheld digital measuring arm with software that stores each reading automatically. Compared with recording manual readings, what is the main benefit?
Readings are stored directly, avoiding transcription errors
Readings no longer need any correlation to other methods
Readings no longer depend on how the part is aligned
Readings are always more accurate than those of a micrometer
Digital systems capture data directly, removing transcription errors and making the data ready for analysis. They do not remove the need for correlation, and alignment still affects the results.
std
II.E.5
A scan of a bracket is aligned to CAD with a best-fit alignment, and every hole reports in tolerance. The drawing specifies datums A, B and C. What is the concern?
It may not reflect the datum reference frame on the drawing
Best-fit alignment is only wrong when the part is made of plastic
Best-fit alignment only affects the color map, not hole positions
Best-fit alignment always gives the same results as datum-based alignment

A best-fit alignment spreads error over the whole part and can make out-of-tolerance features look good; functional results need alignment to the specified datums in order. The software does not do this unless it is told to.
std
II.E.5
A drawing defines datum A by three datum target areas of 5 mm diameter. A vision system measures the part using an automatic plane fit of the whole face. What should the inspector do?
Accept the plane fit, provided the face looks flat in the color map
Set the software to build datum A from the specified target areas only
Accept the plane fit, because the whole face includes the target areas
Use the three highest points the software finds on the whole face
Datum targets restrict which parts of the surface establish the datum, so the software must use only those areas. Fitting the whole face can tilt the datum and shift every measurement made from it.
std
II.E.5
A vision system reports hole positions from edge points it detects in a camera image. Which limitation should the inspector recognize?
Hole positions are always reported to the drawing's datums
Hole positions from a camera cannot be affected by lighting
Burrs, chamfers or lighting can shift the found centers
Hole positions are found by touching each hole with a probe

The software computes centers from edges it finds, so burrs, chamfers, shadows and contrast can move the edge and the center. It reports positions only in the coordinate system it has been set up to use.
std
II.E.5

On a digital measuring system, an inspector sets up a part coordinate system. In the usual right-hand convention, if x runs left to right and y runs front to back across the table, which way does +z point?
Along the table away from the operator
Downward, into the table surface
Along the table toward the operator
Upward, out of the table surface
With x and y on the table plane in a right-hand system, +z is perpendicular to the table, pointing up. Pointing back toward the operator would be along the y axis, not z.
std
II.E.6

A precision spirit level has a sensitivity of 0.02 mm per meter for each division. On a 1.5 m long machine bed, the bubble moves 3 divisions. What is the height difference from one end of the bed to the other?
Height difference = 3 × 0.02 mm/m × 1.5 m = 0.09 mm. Ignoring the 1.5 m length gives 0.06 mm.
std
II.E.6
What does an electronic inclinometer measure?
The height of a surface above a granite plate
The angle between two machined faces of a part
The flatness of a surface across its full length
The angle of a surface relative to gravity
An inclinometer measures tilt relative to the gravity vector, so it shows slope from level. The angle between two part faces is measured with a protractor or sine bar, not with an inclinometer alone.
std
II.E.6
A crew needs to check the slope of a long conveyor frame over 30 m. Which approach suits the task best?
A sine bar laid on the frame with gauge blocks at one end
A laser level projecting a level reference along the frame
A machinist's level moved along the frame and read at one spot only
A bevel protractor set at each end of the frame and compared
A laser projects a level reference over long distances, so heights at points along the frame show its slope. A short level read at one spot shows only local tilt, not the slope over 30 m.
std
II.F.1
A small machine shop checks its gauges only when a reading looks odd. A new quality manager wants a formal calibration system. What is its main purpose?
To reduce how often gauges are used so they wear out more slowly
To keep gauge error known so product decisions can be trusted
To replace the need for any gauge studies such as bias or R&R
To make sure every gauge has a certificate on file for auditors

Calibration compares instruments to traceable standards at planned intervals so their error stays known and acceptable, which is what makes product decisions trustworthy. Having certificates on file is a by-product, not the purpose; a pile of certificates does nothing if gauges drift between them.
std
II.F.1
A calibration lab reviews ten years of records for a group of identical outside micrometers. Every as-found result was well inside tolerance with little drift. What is the most reasonable action?
Lengthen the interval for that group under the lab's documented interval procedure
Shorten the interval, since a gauge that never fails is probably not being checked closely
Keep the interval unchanged, since intervals should not move once they are set
Stop calibrating the group and rely on daily zero checks by the operators

Intervals should be adjusted from evidence; a long history of in-tolerance as-found results supports a longer interval, done under a written procedure. Freezing intervals forever ignores the data that the as-found records exist to provide.
std
II.F.1

A lab's procedure says: if a gauge is found out of tolerance, cut its interval by 50%; if it passes three times in a row, increase the interval by 25%. A torque wrench on a 12-month interval is found out of tolerance today. What is its new interval?
9 months
15 months
6 months
3 months
An out-of-tolerance result triggers the 50% cut, so 12 × 0.5 = 6 months. Nine months comes from applying 25% as a reduction, and 15 months applies the extension rule, which only follows three passes.
std
II.F.1
A certificate shows a reference value of 25.000 mm, a gauge reading of 25.002 mm, and an expanded uncertainty of ±0.003 mm at about 95% confidence. Which statement is best?
The gauge's error is exactly +0.002 mm at that point
The gauge's true error is likely between −0.001 and +0.005 mm
The gauge is out of tolerance because its error is not zero
The uncertainty shows the reference standard was itself faulty

The observed error is +0.002 mm, and the uncertainty widens it to a range: 0.002 − 0.003 = −0.001 to 0.002 + 0.003 = +0.005 mm. Treating +0.002 as exact ignores the uncertainty that every measurement, including a calibration, carries.
std
II.F.1
A lab reports a gauge error of +0.004 mm against an allowable error of ±0.005 mm, with an expanded uncertainty of ±0.003 mm. What is the best interpretation?
The gauge plainly passes, since 0.004 mm is smaller than 0.005 mm
The uncertainty can be ignored because it is smaller than the allowable error
The error should be reported as +0.001 mm after subtracting the uncertainty
Conformance cannot be stated with high confidence

Because the uncertainty range (+0.001 to +0.007 mm) straddles the +0.005 mm limit, a pass cannot be stated with high confidence; the lab's decision rule (for example, guard bands) must settle it. Calling it a plain pass ignores the reason uncertainty is reported at all.
std
II.F.1
A gauge crib keeps a calibration log so it can recall gauges before they come due. Which set of entries does the recall process depend on most?
Each gauge's purchase price, supplier and warranty end date
Each gauge's color, storage drawer size and manufacturer catalog number
Each gauge's operator name, shift and part numbers it measured last week
Each gauge's ID, current location, last calibration date and due date
To recall a gauge on time you must know which gauge it is, where it is, and when it is due. Usage details help with trace-back after a failure, but they do not drive the recall schedule.
std
II.F.1
An inspector picks up a caliper whose calibration sticker shows a due date that passed last week. The caliper reads zero correctly. What should she do?
Use it for today's job, since it zeroes and looks undamaged
Write a new due date on the sticker and notify the lab later
Pull it for recalibration and use a current gauge
Use it, then re-measure today's parts once the caliper is recalibrated

An overdue gauge has unknown status and should be pulled from use; a correct zero says nothing about error elsewhere in the range. Using it and re-measuring later spends inspection effort on a gauge that should not be in service.
std
II.F.1
A dial indicator carries a label reading "Limited calibration: 0 to 5 mm only." An inspector needs to measure a runout that may reach 8 mm. What should he do?
Use the indicator, since most of its travel was verified
Use the indicator and add a note that readings above 5 mm are estimates
Ask the lab to remove the label so the indicator can be used fully
Use a different instrument that is calibrated over the needed range
A limited-calibration label restricts use to the verified range; readings outside it have no known accuracy. Adding a note does not make an unverified reading acceptable for an inspection decision.
std
II.F.1

A plant has about 3,000 gauges spread across many cells. It wants a handheld reader to detect all the tagged gauges in a closed plastic cabinet in one pass, without aiming at each one. Which identification method fits?
Barcode labels
RFID tags
Engraved serial numbers
Color-coded stickers
RFID tags are read by radio signal, so many can be read at once without line of sight. Barcodes need a clear line of sight and are scanned one at a time.
std
II.F.1
A gauge crib replaces a handwritten sign-out sheet with barcode labels scanned when each gauge is issued and returned. What is the main benefit?
Fast, error-free capture of which gauge went to which job
Each label shows the gauge's calibration status without needing any database
Gauges can be read inside closed metal drawers without opening them
Each gauge no longer needs a unique number once it carries a barcode

A barcode encodes the gauge ID; scanning it links the gauge to a database record quickly and without transcription errors. The label itself does not hold calibration status, and barcodes need line of sight.
std
II.F.1
Two identical 0–25 mm micrometers in a cell are both labeled only "0–25 MIC." One is later found out of tolerance. What problem does the labeling create?
The lab cannot calibrate either micrometer until new labels are added
The out-of-tolerance result cannot be tied to the parts that micrometer measured
Both micrometers must be scrapped, because identical gauges cannot be calibrated
The cell must switch to RFID before any product evaluation can start

Without a unique ID, records cannot show which micrometer measured which parts, so trace-back after a failure is guesswork. Any durable unique code would solve this; RFID is one option, not a precondition.
std
II.F.2
Which list runs from the highest level of the measurement standards hierarchy to the lowest?
National standards, international standards, working standards, reference standards, shop gauges
International standards, national standards, reference standards, working standards, shop gauges
Reference standards, international standards, national standards, working standards, shop gauges
International standards, reference standards, national standards, shop gauges, working standards

Traceability flows down from the international definitions of the units, through national standards, to a lab's reference standards, then working standards, then the gauges used on product. Putting national above international reverses the top of the chain.
std
II.F.2
A set of gauge blocks kept in the inspection area is used every day to set and check micrometers. In the standards hierarchy, this set is best described as:
International standards
National standards
Working standards
Reference standards
Standards used routinely to check or calibrate shop instruments are working standards. Reference standards sit above them and are used mainly to calibrate the working set.
std
II.F.2
A calibration lab keeps one set of gauge blocks locked away and uses it only to calibrate its everyday working blocks. Why?
Limiting its use reduces wear, so it stays accurate enough to check working blocks
Locked blocks need no calibration of their own, which saves the lab outside fees
Customers require that any gauge blocks used on product be stored in a locked cabinet
Keeping a spare set allows the lab to skip calibrating its working blocks each cycle
A reference set is protected from daily wear and handling so it stays more accurate than the working set it is used to check. It still needs its own periodic calibration to stay traceable.
std
II.F.2
A calibration lab wants its reference standards to be traceable. What is the usual next link above them in the chain?
Comparison with the newest working standards bought from the same maker
A statement of accuracy from the manufacturer's catalog for each standard
Comparison with a second set of reference standards kept in the same lab
Calibration by an accredited lab or the national metrology institute, with stated uncertainty

Reference standards are calibrated by a higher-level accredited lab or the national metrology institute, which holds the national standards. Comparing them with other standards at the same or lower level adds no traceability.
std
II.F.2
A part measured by a supplier in one country is re-measured by its customer in another country. What ultimately allows the two results to be compared?
Both labs use gauges built by the same instrument manufacturer
Both labs follow the same internal calibration interval procedure
Each national standard is linked to the SI units through international comparisons
Each lab averages its readings over more trials than the other
Measurements become comparable worldwide because national standards are tied to the SI definitions through international comparisons. Using the same instrument brand does not create traceability.
std
II.F.2
A supplier states its height gauge is "traceable." Which document best supports that claim?
A sticker on the gauge showing the date its next calibration is due
A calibration certificate listing the standards used and the uncertainty
The manufacturer's catalog page listing the gauge's stated accuracy
A purchase receipt showing the gauge was bought brand new earlier this year

Traceability needs a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each with stated uncertainty; a certificate that identifies the standards and their own traceability provides that link. A due-date sticker shows status, not the chain behind it.
std
II.F.2

During an audit, an inspector learns that the certificate for a lab's reference gauge blocks expired 18 months ago and they have not been recalibrated since. What does this mean for the working gauges calibrated with those blocks?
Their traceability is in doubt, because one link in the chain is not current
Nothing changes, since gauge blocks are steel and do not change size over time
Their traceability is intact as long as their own stickers are still current
They must be scrapped, because untraceable gauges cannot be recalibrated

Traceability holds only when every link has current, valid calibration; an expired reference standard breaks the chain for everything calibrated from it. The working gauges can be recalibrated once valid standards are used, so scrapping them is not required.
std
II.F.2
A technician finds a micrometer reading +0.008 mm at 25 mm, adjusts it, and it then reads +0.001 mm. What should the calibration record show?
Only the +0.001 mm reading, since that is how the micrometer leaves the lab
Only the +0.008 mm reading, since the adjustment is noted elsewhere
The +0.008 mm reading before adjustment and the +0.001 mm reading after
The average of the two readings, +0.0045 mm, as the reported error

Both are needed: the as-found result shows whether product measured before the visit may be affected, and the as-left result shows the condition in which the gauge returns to use. Recording only the as-left value hides the evidence needed for any product impact review.
std
II.F.2
A height gauge goes for repair after its scale is damaged. Which reading tells the quality engineer whether parts measured since its last calibration might be affected?
The as-left reading taken after the repair is finished
The reading taken at the next scheduled calibration
The accuracy stated in the manufacturer's specification
The as-found reading taken before the repair
Only the as-found reading reflects the condition the gauge was in while it measured product. The as-left reading describes the gauge after repair, so it says nothing about past measurements.
std
II.F.3
A 100 mm steel gauge block is measured at 26 °C instead of the 20 °C reference temperature. Using a coefficient of 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, about how much longer is it than at 20 °C?
Growth = 100 × 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ × (26 − 20) = 0.0069 mm. 0.0299 mm uses 26 °C instead of the 6 °C difference, and 0.0012 mm is the growth for only one degree.
std
II.F.3
A set of gauge blocks arrives from an unheated receiving dock on a cold morning. The technician wants to calibrate it right away. What should happen first?
Warm the blocks with a heat gun so they reach lab temperature quickly
Calibrate at once and correct the results using the dock temperature
Calibrate at once, since steel blocks change size only at high temperatures
Let the blocks soak in the lab until they reach the controlled temperature

Gauges and standards must stabilize at the lab's controlled temperature before calibration, or thermal size change will appear as error. Forced heating creates uneven temperatures and still leaves the blocks out of equilibrium.
std
II.F.3
A calibration lab's humidity control fails and relative humidity stays high for several weeks. Which effect on its steel gauge blocks is the main concern?
Corrosion that damages the measuring faces and changes their size
Thermal growth caused by the moisture held in the surrounding air
Magnetism that builds up in the steel when the air is damp
Loss of hardness as water is slowly absorbed into the steel

High humidity promotes rust and corrosion on steel standards, which damages lapped faces and alters dimensions. Size change from temperature is a separate effect; moisture in the air does not make steel grow.
std
II.F.3
A lab places a high-magnification electronic comparator next to a wall shared with a stamping press. Readings drift and jump whenever the press runs. What is the most likely cause and fix?
Electrical noise from the press; replace the comparator's power cord
Operator fatigue from press noise; rotate technicians more often
Vibration from the press; isolate the comparator or move it away
Temperature swings from the press; recalibrate the comparator daily

Readings that change in step with a nearby press point to vibration, which a sensitive instrument picks up directly; isolation mounts or relocation address it. Recalibrating daily would not remove an environmental disturbance that exists during measurement.
std
II.F.3
Before calibrating a micrometer, a technician skips cleaning the anvil and spindle faces. What is the likely effect?
Dirt particles slightly lower the readings and protect the faces from wear
