Particles between the faces add to the readings and can scratch the faces
There is no effect, since the micrometer's ratchet makes up for any dirt
The readings will be correct but will be harder to repeat on the next trial

Any film or particle between the measuring faces adds thickness to the reading and can scratch the faces, so cleaning comes before calibration. The ratchet controls measuring force; it cannot remove the thickness of debris.
std
II.F.4
A part has a specification of 10.00 ± 0.05 mm. Its gauge is later found to read 0.02 mm lower than the true value. Which accepted parts are most at risk of actually being out of specification?
Accepted parts recorded above 10.03 mm
Accepted parts recorded below 9.97 mm
Accepted parts recorded between 9.97 and 10.03 mm
Accepted parts recorded above 10.05 mm

True value = reading + 0.02, so a part recorded above 10.03 mm may truly exceed 10.05 mm. Parts recorded below 9.97 mm are actually larger than recorded, which moves them toward the middle of the tolerance, not out of it.
std
II.F.4
The GO member of a plug gauge used to accept holes is found worn undersize. What is the main risk to the customer?
Good holes were rejected and scrapped without need
The gauge will now reject every hole it checks
Oversize holes were sent back for extra machining
Some undersize holes may have been accepted and shipped

A worn-small GO plug enters holes that are below the minimum size, so undersize holes can pass (a false accept), which is the risk that reaches the customer. False rejects cost money internally but do not ship bad parts.
std
II.F.4
The calibration lab reports that a thread plug gauge was found out of tolerance at its as-found check. What should be done first?
Adjust or replace the gauge and return it to the line right away
Note the result and wait for the next audit to review the impact
Increase the gauge's calibration interval to avoid a repeat finding
Tag it out of service and assess the product it accepted

The gauge must not be used, and the product it accepted since its last good calibration must be assessed for risk. Returning a replacement to the line fixes the future but leaves possibly nonconforming product unexamined.
std
II.F.4
A gauge passed calibration in March and was found out of tolerance in June. Records show it was used on lots in April, May and June. Which lots should be evaluated?
Only the lots measured in June, the month it was found bad
All lots measured with the gauge since the March calibration
Only lots that customers have complained about so far
A random sample of lots from the whole year

The last known good point is the March calibration; the gauge could have gone out at any time after that, so every lot it measured since then is suspect. Waiting for complaints shifts the detection job to the customer.
std
II.F.4
After a micrometer is found out of tolerance, a technician recalibrates it. What must happen before it goes back into service?
Its as-left results must pass and its status label must be updated
It must be used on three lots in parallel with another gauge to prove it
Its interval must be doubled so it is checked less often in the future
It must be held for one full interval to confirm it does not drift again

A recalibrated instrument returns to use once the as-left results meet requirements and its status identification is current. Parallel use or holding it a full interval are not standard requirements, and doubling the interval after a failure is the wrong direction.
std
II.F.4
An evaluation after an out-of-calibration finding shows that some product already shipped may not meet specification. What action is required?
Wait to see whether the customer reports any field failures
Notify the customer and treat the lots as nonconforming
Replace the gauge and note the finding in the next management review
Ship extra parts to the customer without explaining the reason

When nonconforming product may have shipped, the customer must be told so they can act, and the product handled under the nonconformance process. Replacing the gauge without telling the customer leaves suspect product in use.
std
II.F.4
The same caliper has been found out of tolerance at its last three calibrations. Besides evaluating product each time, what should the organization do?
Keep the interval and accept that this caliper drifts more than others
Lengthen the interval so the caliper spends less time out of service
Investigate the cause and review the interval and suitability of the gauge
Remove the calibration sticker so the caliper is used only for rough checks

Repeat failures call for corrective action: find the cause (wear, misuse, wrong gauge for the job) and shorten the interval or change the instrument. Simply accepting the drift leaves the same product risk in place each cycle.
std
II.G.1
In measurement system analysis, bias is best defined as:
The spread of repeated readings on the same part by one operator
The average reading minus the reference value
The change in a gauge's readings over a long period of time
The variation in average readings between different operators
Bias is the systematic offset between the observed average and the reference (true) value. The spread of repeated readings by one operator is repeatability, a precision measure.
std
II.G.1
A reference part certified at 20.000 mm is measured five times: 20.004, 20.006, 20.003, 20.005 and 20.007 mm. What is the bias?
The average is 20.005 mm, so bias = 20.005 − 20.000 = +0.005 mm. −0.005 mm reverses the sign (reference minus average), and +0.004 mm is the range of the readings.
std
II.G.1
A gauge has a known, stable bias of +0.005 mm across its range. A part reads 12.340 mm. What is the best estimate of its true size?
Positive bias means the gauge reads high, so true value ≈ reading − bias = 12.340 − 0.005 = 12.335 mm. Adding the bias moves the estimate the wrong way.
std
II.G.1
An operator measures a master ring 25 times and finds the readings tightly grouped but all slightly above its certified value. Which characteristic does this mainly show?
Poor reproducibility
Poor repeatability
Poor stability
Bias
A consistent offset of the readings from the reference value is bias. Tight grouping means repeatability is good, so a repeatability problem is ruled out.
std
II.G.2
In MSA, the stability of a measurement system refers to:
How close its readings are to the reference value at one time
How much its bias changes across the gauge's operating range
How much its results on the same master change over time
How closely two operators agree when measuring the same part
Stability (drift) is the change in measurements of the same master or part over an extended period. Change across the operating range is linearity, not stability.
std
II.G.2
A quality technician wants to check a CMM's stability. Which approach fits best?
Measure ten production parts once each and compare the results to drawing limits
Have three operators measure the same part twice and compare their averages
Measure reference parts at the low, middle and high end of the range in one day
Measure the same master part a few times each day and plot the results on a control chart

Stability is shown by repeated measurement of a stable master over time, charted so drift or shifts appear as signals. Measuring parts across the range in one day studies linearity, not change over time.
std
II.G.2
A control chart of daily readings on the same master gauge block shows the average rising steadily over three weeks, while the daily ranges stay small. What does this indicate?
A stability problem: the system's readings drift over time
A repeatability problem: readings within each day vary too much
A reproducibility problem: operators disagree with each other
A linearity problem: bias differs between small and large sizes
A steady trend in the averages for the same master means bias is changing over time, which is a stability issue. Small daily ranges show that short-term repeatability is fine.
std
II.G.3
Precision of a measurement system describes:
How close the average reading is to the true value
How closely repeated readings of one item agree
How finely the instrument's display or scale is divided
How well the gauge's bias stays constant over a long period
Precision is the closeness of agreement among repeated measurements, regardless of where they fall relative to the true value. Closeness to the true value is accuracy.
std
II.G.3
Five repeated readings of one pin are 5.02, 5.04, 5.03, 5.05 and 5.01 mm. Using the sample standard deviation as the measure of precision, what is it?
The mean is 5.03 mm; squared deviations sum to 0.0010, so s = √(0.0010 / 4) ≈ 0.016 mm. 0.014 mm divides by n instead of n − 1, and 0.040 mm is the range.
std
II.G.3
In a typical MSA, the precision (measurement variation) of a gauging system is broken into which two components?
Bias and linearity
Accuracy and stability
Repeatability and reproducibility
Resolution and calibration uncertainty

Measurement system precision is usually split into repeatability (equipment variation) and reproducibility (appraiser variation), which together make up GRR. Bias and linearity describe location errors, not spread.
std
II.G.4
Accuracy of a measurement system is best described as:
The smallest change in size that the instrument can display
The agreement between operators measuring the same part
The closeness of measured values to the reference value
The closeness of repeated readings to one another
Accuracy is how close measurements come to the true or accepted reference value. The closeness of repeated readings to one another is precision.
std
II.G.4
Gauge A gives readings on a 10.000 mm master of 10.011, 10.012, 10.011 and 10.012 mm. Gauge B gives 9.992, 10.008, 9.995 and 10.005 mm. Which statement is correct?
A is more precise, while B is more accurate on average
A is both more accurate and more precise than B
B is more precise, while A is more accurate on average
B is both more accurate and more precise than A

A's readings are tightly grouped but average about 10.0115 mm, so it is precise but biased; B's average is exactly 10.000 mm but its readings spread widely. Calling A more accurate confuses tight grouping with closeness to the true value.
std
II.G.4
A gauge's readings are tightly grouped but consistently 0.010 mm above the reference value. Which action most directly improves its accuracy?
Calibrate and adjust the gauge to remove the offset
Have more operators measure each part and average them
Take more readings per part to tighten the grouping
Replace the gauge with one that has finer resolution
The problem is a systematic offset, which calibration and adjustment remove. More readings or more operators reduce the effect of random variation but leave a constant offset untouched.
std
II.G.5
Linearity of a measurement system refers to:
The change in bias over the operating range of the gauge
The change in bias over a long period of time
The spread of readings when one operator repeats a measurement
The straightness of the gauge's measuring surfaces
Linearity is how bias differs across the gauge's range, such as small at the low end and larger at the high end. Change in bias over time is stability.
std
II.G.5
A linearity study finds a bias of +0.002 mm on a 5 mm reference and +0.010 mm on a 25 mm reference. If bias changes linearly, what bias would you expect at 15 mm?
Bias rises 0.008 mm over 20 mm, or 0.0004 mm per mm; at 15 mm it is 0.002 + 0.0004 × 10 = +0.006 mm. +0.008 mm is the total change in bias, not the bias at 15 mm.
std
II.G.5
A team wants to check the linearity of a height gauge used from 0 to 300 mm. Which study design fits best?
Measure one 150 mm master many times over several weeks and chart the averages
Have three operators measure ten production parts three times each
Measure several reference standards spread across 0 to 300 mm and compare bias at each
Measure one 300 mm master many times and compute the bias at that size

Linearity needs bias at several known sizes covering the range, so the change in bias can be seen or fitted to a line. Measuring one master over time studies stability, and one size alone cannot show how bias changes.
std
II.G.5
A study finds the same bias of +0.003 mm on reference parts at the low, middle and high end of a gauge's range. What does this show?
The gauge has a linearity problem but no bias
The gauge has a stability problem over its range
The gauge has poor repeatability at every size
The gauge has bias but no linearity problem

A constant bias across the range means the bias does not change with size, so linearity is good even though a bias exists to be corrected. A linearity problem would show bias changing from one end of the range to the other.
std
II.G.6
In a gauge R&R study, repeatability is the variation seen when:
Different operators measure the same parts with the same gauge
The same operator measures one part several times with one gauge
The same master is measured once a day over several weeks
Reference parts of different sizes are measured across the range
Repeatability (equipment variation) is within-operator variation from repeated trials on the same part with the same gauge. Variation between different operators is reproducibility.
std
II.G.6
In a gauge R&R study, reproducibility is mainly the variation:
In repeated readings by one operator on one part
Between the gauge's average reading and the reference value
Between the average readings of different operators on the same parts
Among the parts themselves, as produced by the process
Reproducibility (appraiser variation) is the difference in averages between operators measuring the same parts with the same gauge. Repeated readings by one operator describe repeatability.
std
II.G.6
An R&R study shows that reproducibility is much larger than repeatability. Which action is most likely to help?
Repair or replace the gauge's worn measuring faces
Recalibrate the gauge at a shorter interval
Standardize the method and train operators to use it
Buy a gauge with finer resolution for the cell

Large reproducibility means operators get different averages, which usually points to differences in technique, so a standard method and training address it. Worn faces would mainly inflate repeatability.
std
II.G.6
An R&R study shows that repeatability is much larger than reproducibility. Where should the team look first?
At differences in how each operator reads the scale
At the part-to-part variation produced by the process
At the operators' training records and work instructions
At the gauge itself: wear, play or fixturing
Large repeatability (equipment variation) points to the instrument or its setup, such as wear, play or poor part location. Operator technique differences show up mainly as reproducibility.
std
II.G.6
An R&R study gives a combined measurement standard deviation (σGRR) of 0.004 mm. The part tolerance is 0.120 mm. Using 6σ for %GRR to tolerance, what is the result and the usual interpretation?
3.3%, so the gauge is clearly acceptable
20%, so it may be acceptable depending on the application
20%, so the gauge is unacceptable and must be replaced
40%, so the gauge is unacceptable and must be replaced

%GRR = 6 × 0.004 / 0.120 = 20%; common guidelines treat under 10% as acceptable, 10% to 30% as possibly acceptable depending on importance and cost, and over 30% as unacceptable. 3.3% leaves out the factor of 6.
std
II.G.6
In an R&R study, repeatability is σ = 0.003 mm and reproducibility is σ = 0.004 mm. What is σGRR?
Independent variances add: σGRR = √(0.003² + 0.004²) = √0.000025 = 0.005 mm. Adding the standard deviations directly (0.007 mm) overstates the combined variation.
std
II.G.6
In an R&R study, the parts are coded and presented in random order so operators cannot see their earlier readings. Why?
So operators are not swayed by remembering earlier readings
So the study needs fewer parts and fewer trials to finish
So the gauge does not need to be calibrated before the study
So that each operator measures different parts from the others

Blind, randomized measurement keeps operators from steering readings toward what they recorded before, which would understate the real variation. All operators still measure the same parts; that is how reproducibility is estimated.
std
II.G.6
A team plans an R&R study for a caliper used on a shaft diameter. How should it choose the parts?
Pick parts from the tightest part of the process so readings are consistent
Pick parts that cover the range of variation the process normally produces
Pick one master part and measure it many times by each operator
Pick only rejected parts so the study focuses on problem sizes

Parts should represent the process spread so the study shows how well the gauge separates parts that really differ. Picking only very similar parts makes the gauge look worse relative to part variation and does not reflect real use.
std
III.A.1
A title block states: unless otherwise specified, .XX ±.01 and .XXX ±.005. A dimension on the view reads 1.250 with no tolerance. What are its limits?
A three-place decimal takes the .XXX tolerance of ±.005, giving 1.245 to 1.255. Using ±.01 applies the two-place tolerance to a three-place dimension.
std
III.A.1
The title block says all dimensions are in millimeters. A feature dimensioned 25 ±0.1 measures 0.984 in on an inch micrometer. What should the inspector conclude?
It cannot be judged until a metric micrometer is used
It is oversize, because 0.984 in is about 25.10 mm
It is undersize, because 0.984 is below the 25 lower limit
It conforms, because 0.984 in is about 24.99 mm
Converting 0.984 × 25.4 gives 24.994 mm, inside 24.9 to 25.1. Comparing the raw inch reading with millimeter limits ignores the unit stated in the title block.
std
III.A.1
Which information is normally recorded in a drawing's revision block?
Part number, sheet count and the drawing scale
Datum features and their order of precedence
Material, finish and the general tolerance values
Revision letter, change description, date and approval
The revision block is the change history: what changed, under which revision letter, when and who approved it. Material, part number, scale and general tolerances belong in the title block.
std
III.A.1

Parts arrive for inspection with a router calling for revision C. The controlled drawing on file is at revision D, and its revision block shows that D added a chamfer. What should the inspector do first?
Inspect to revision C because the router lists it
Inspect to revision D because it is the latest drawing
Inspect to both and accept parts meeting either one
Hold the job and have the revision mismatch resolved

A conflict between the router and the controlled drawing has to be settled by whoever controls the order and the design before acceptance. Simply using the latest drawing may be wrong if the order is contractually tied to revision C.
std
III.A.1
A general note reads "Break all sharp edges 0.2–0.5 mm." No edge break appears on any view. How should the inspector treat it?
A requirement on every edge, checked like a dimension
As applying only where an edge break is shown on a view
As a machinist instruction that falls outside inspection
As guidance only, since notes carry no inspection weight
General notes are part of the product definition and apply wherever they are not overridden, so the edge break must be checked. A note does not need a callout on a view to be binding.
std
III.A.1
A drawing view is marked SCALE 2:1. What does this mean?
Two views of the part share one sheet
The view is drawn half the actual size
Each dimension carries twice the tolerance
The view is drawn twice the actual size
The first number is the drawing size and the second the actual size, so 2:1 is an enlarged view. Reading it as half size reverses the ratio.
std
III.A.1
A feature on an older drawing has no dimension. An operator suggests measuring the print with a rule and applying the scale. What should the inspector do?
Ask the design owner to define the missing dimension
Measure several parts and use their average as nominal
Accept the feature since it has no stated requirement
Scale the print and apply the title block tolerance

Prints shrink, stretch and are drawn to limited accuracy, so scaling a drawing is not a valid way to set a requirement. An undimensioned feature is a drawing problem for the design authority, not something to accept by default.
std
III.A.1
A dimension on a drawing is shown in parentheses as (42.5). How should the inspector treat it?
As a reference dimension, not used for acceptance
As a critical dimension that needs 100% checking
As a basic dimension, held to the frame tolerance
As a dimension held to the title block tolerance
Parentheses mark a reference dimension, which is for information and is usually derived from other dimensions. A basic dimension is shown in a box, not in parentheses.
std
III.A.1
A drawing shows "4X Ø6.0 ±0.1" pointing to one hole in a bolt pattern. What does this callout require?
Four holes with a combined size of 24.0 ±0.4
One hole of Ø5.9 to Ø6.1, at the leader only
Four holes, but only the one labeled is checked
Four holes, each Ø5.9 to Ø6.1
The "4X" means the requirement applies to four identical features, and each must meet the size. It does not pool the size across holes or limit inspection to the hole the leader touches.
std
III.A.1
A customer sends a 3D model with product and manufacturing information (PMI) and no 2D drawing. Where should the inspector look for the tolerances?
In the last 2D drawing issued for the part
In the geometry's modeled size, with no tolerance
In the supplier's standard shop tolerances
In the PMI annotations within the model
In model based definition the annotated model is the authority, and its PMI carries dimensions, tolerances and notes. An old 2D drawing may be obsolete and has no standing once the model governs.
std
III.A.1
What is a main inspection benefit of model based definition?
CMM programs can be built from the model data
Inspectors can scale features from the model view
Tolerances are no longer needed for most features
Revision control no longer applies to the part
Because nominal geometry and tolerances are machine readable, inspection programs can be built from the model with less retyping. MBD still needs tolerances and revision control.
std
III.A.2
A drawing uses third-angle projection. Where is the top view placed relative to the front view?
To its right
Below it
To its left
Above it
In third-angle projection each view is placed on the side it is seen from, so the top view sits above the front view. Placing it below is the first-angle convention.
std
III.A.2
An inspector used to third-angle drawings receives one with the first-angle symbol in the title block. What must he keep in mind?
The view drawn to the right of the front is the left side
The view drawn to the right of the front is the right side
Hidden lines are left off in first-angle drawings
Dimensions are taken from the opposite datum face
In first-angle projection the left-side view is placed to the right of the front view, the reverse of third-angle. Projection angle changes view placement, not line conventions or datums.
std
III.A.2
A front view shows a cutting-plane line labeled A-A with arrows. What does section A-A show?
Interior features exposed by a cut along line A-A
The true shape of a sloped surface, seen square to it
The outside of the part seen from opposite the arrows
An enlarged view of the circled area near line A-A

A section view shows interior features exposed by the cutting plane, looking in the arrow direction. An enlarged circled area is a detail view, and a true-shape view of an inclined face is an auxiliary view.
std
III.A.2
A bracket has a face at 30° to the main views, and a hole in that face looks elliptical in every principal view. Which view shows the hole's true shape?
A detail view of the hole at an enlarged scale
A rear view projected opposite to the front view
A section view taken through the center of the hole
An auxiliary view square to the inclined face
An auxiliary view is projected perpendicular to an inclined surface, so features on it appear true size and shape. Enlarging the hole in a detail view would still show it foreshortened.
std
III.A.2
A drawing note says "Plate per SPEC-220." The inspector has no copy of SPEC-220. What should she do?
Get the controlled revision of SPEC-220 before judging plating
Reject the parts because the drawing gives no plating values
Accept the plating if it looks even and free of blisters
Ask the plating operator what SPEC-220 normally requires

A referenced specification is part of the requirement, so the inspector needs the current controlled copy to know what to check. A visual check or an operator's memory does not establish the requirement.
std
III.A.2
What does a dimension enclosed in a rectangle mean under ASME Y14.5?
A reference dimension shown for information and not inspected
A critical dimension that must be checked on every part
A basic dimension, the exact value a tolerance zone is located from
A dimension that takes the title block tolerance by default
A basic dimension is a theoretically exact value; its permitted variation comes from a feature control frame. Reference dimensions are shown in parentheses, not boxes.
std
III.A.2
Which of these is a feature of size?
A single flat mounting face
A curved cam profile
A chamfered outer edge
A Ø8 cylindrical hole
A feature of size has opposed points or surfaces, such as a cylinder or a slot width, so it has a size that can be measured. A single flat face has no opposing element.
std
III.A.2
A shaft is dimensioned Ø19.95–20.00. What is its least material condition (LMC)?
For an external feature, least material is the smallest size, Ø19.95. Ø20.00 is the MMC, where the shaft contains the most material.
std
III.A.2
A hole is dimensioned Ø10.0–10.2. What is its maximum material condition (MMC)?
An internal feature has the most material when the hole is smallest, so MMC is Ø10.0. Ø10.2 is the LMC, the largest hole.
std
III.A.2
A position tolerance in a feature control frame has no material condition modifier after it. Under current Y14.5 practice, how does it apply?
Only when the feature is at its nominal size
Regardless of feature size, so no bonus is allowed
At MMC by default, so bonus is allowed as size departs
At LMC by default, so bonus grows as the feature fills
With no modifier, a tolerance applies regardless of feature size (RFS), and the zone stays the same at any produced size. MMC must be shown with the circled M to permit bonus.

III.A.2
Which geometric tolerance is never related to a datum?
Position
Flatness
Perpendicularity
Total runout
Form tolerances such as flatness control a feature against itself, so no datum is referenced. Perpendicularity, position and runout all need a datum.

III.A.2
Parallelism, perpendicularity and angularity belong to which category of geometric tolerance?
Orientation
Form
Location
Runout
These three control the tilt of a feature relative to a datum, which is orientation. Form tolerances use no datum, and location controls position, not tilt.

III.A.2
A surface is held to 10.0 ±0.2 thick and has a flatness callout of 0.1. All thickness readings are within limits, but flatness measures 0.15. What should the inspector conclude?
The part conforms because size is within its ±0.2 limits
The part needs a deviation since the callouts conflict
The part conforms because 0.15 is less than the 0.4 size range
The part is nonconforming because flatness is exceeded
A flatness callout refines the form allowed by the size tolerance, so it must be met on its own. Passing size does not excuse a separate, tighter form requirement.
std
III.A.2
How should this feature control frame be read: [position | Ø0.25 (M) | A | B | C]?
Position within a Ø0.25 zone RFS, datum C set up first
Position within a 0.25 square zone at MMC, datums in any order
Position within a Ø0.25 zone at MMC, datums in order A, B, C
Position within ±0.25 coordinates at MMC, datums in order A, B, C
The diameter symbol makes the zone cylindrical, the circled M sets MMC, and datums are applied left to right as primary, secondary and tertiary. Datum order is not optional.

III.A.3
A hole has a position tolerance of Ø0.008 RFS. A CMM reports the hole center 0.003 off in X and 0.004 off in Y from true position. What is the actual position, and is it acceptable?
Ø0.005, accept
Ø0.007, accept
Ø0.010, reject
Ø0.014, reject
Actual position = 2 × √(0.003² + 0.004²) = 2 × 0.005 = Ø0.010, which exceeds Ø0.008. Ø0.005 is the radial offset and forgets to double it to a diameter.
std
III.A.3
A pin's center is measured 0.03 mm off in X and 0.04 mm off in Y from true position. What is its actual position as a diameter?
2 × √(0.03² + 0.04²) = 2 × 0.05 = Ø0.10. Adding the offsets (0.07) treats a diagonal distance as a straight sum.
std
III.A.3
A ±0.05 coordinate tolerance on a hole location is converted to a cylindrical position zone that just contains the old square zone. What diameter is that?
The square zone's corner is √(0.05² + 0.05²) = 0.0707 from center, so the circle through the corners is Ø0.141. Ø0.100 only matches the square's width and misses its corners.
std
III.A.3
A hole is Ø10.00–10.20 with a position tolerance of Ø0.10 at MMC. The hole measures Ø10.12. What total position tolerance is allowed?
Bonus = actual size − MMC = 10.12 − 10.00 = 0.12, so the total is 0.10 + 0.12 = Ø0.22. Ø0.30 adds the full size range, which only applies at LMC.
std
III.A.3
A pin is Ø7.90–8.00 with a position tolerance of Ø0.05 at MMC. The pin measures Ø7.94. What total position tolerance is allowed?
For an external feature MMC is the largest size, so bonus = 8.00 − 7.94 = 0.06 and the total is Ø0.11. Ø0.15 adds the whole size tolerance, as if the pin were at LMC.
std
III.A.3
A hole is Ø.250–.260 with a position tolerance of Ø.010 at MMC. It measures Ø.256 and is .005 off in X and .006 off in Y. What is the correct decision?
Accept: actual Ø.0156 is within Ø.016 allowed
Reject: actual Ø.0156 exceeds the Ø.010 allowed
Reject: actual Ø.022 exceeds the Ø.016 allowed
Accept: actual Ø.011 is within the Ø.020 allowed
Actual position is 2 × √(.005² + .006²) = Ø.0156, and bonus .006 raises the allowance to Ø.016, so the hole passes. Rejecting against Ø.010 ignores the MMC bonus.
std
III.A.3
A hole's position callout is Ø0.10 with no modifier. The hole is 0.08 larger than its minimum size. An inspector allows Ø0.18 and accepts a hole at Ø0.15 actual position. What is wrong?
Bonus applies, but should be taken from LMC rather than from MMC
No bonus applies without the MMC modifier, so it should be rejected
Nothing, since bonus always applies to holes made above minimum
The bonus should be 0.04, half the size departure, so it still passes
Without a material condition modifier the tolerance is RFS and stays Ø0.10 at any size, so Ø0.15 fails. Bonus is a feature of MMC (or LMC) callouts, not of holes in general.
std
III.A.4
A feature control frame references datums A | B | C, all planar. In a proper setup, what is the minimum number of contact points with the secondary datum?
Two
One
Three
Six
The 3-2-1 principle gives the primary datum at least three points, the secondary two and the tertiary one. Three points belongs to the primary.
std
III.A.4
For a prismatic part, how many degrees of freedom does the primary datum plane constrain?
Six: all translations and rotations
Two: one translation and one rotation only
One: translation normal to the plane
Three: one translation and two rotations
Seating on a plane stops movement into it and rotation about the two axes lying in it, three degrees in all. The secondary and tertiary datums constrain the rest.
std
III.A.4
A frame calls datums A | B | C. An inspector pushes the part against the B fence first and then lowers it onto the A surface plate. Why is this a problem?
Nothing, because the part touches both datums in the end
The tertiary datum C should have been seated first instead
Precedence is reversed, so the part may seat wrongly
Datum order only matters when parts are checked on a CMM
Datum order sets which surface dominates when the part is not perfect; seating B first can tilt the part off A and change results. Ending in contact with both does not guarantee the same alignment.
std
III.A.4
Primary datum A is a Ø20 bore referenced RFS. Which simulator best sets up the part?
A fixed pin sized at the bore's maximum material size
A fixed pin sized at the bore's least material size
An expanding mandrel fitted to the actual bore
Three point contacts on the face that surrounds the bore
At RFS the datum axis comes from the actual mating size of the bore, which an expanding mandrel finds. A fixed pin at MMC size is the simulator for a datum referenced at MMC.
std
III.A.4
On a CMM, why should the part coordinate system be built from the datum features named on the drawing?
It shortens the program compared with using machine axes
It removes the need to measure the datum features at all
Datum features are always the smoothest surfaces on the part
Results then reflect the reference frame the design specifies
Tolerances are defined relative to the datum reference frame, so measuring from any other alignment can pass bad parts or fail good ones. Speed and surface finish are not the reason.

III.B.1
Which statement best describes the acceptance quality limit (AQL)?
The poorest process average judged acceptable for a series of lots
The average outgoing quality after rejected lots are sorted
The quality level at which lots are rejected most of the time
The highest percent nonconforming any single accepted lot may hold
An AQL is a process-average level tied to a series of lots, and lots at the AQL are accepted most of the time. It is not a ceiling on each accepted lot; plans can accept lots worse than the AQL.
std
III.B.1
A buyer says, "With an AQL of 1.0, no lot we accept will be worse than 1% nonconforming." What is the best correction?
An AQL of 1.0 means one defect is allowed in the sample
Lots at 1% are mostly accepted, but worse lots can still pass
Correct, because the plan rejects any lot above 1% defects
An AQL of 1.0 means 1% of lots will be wrongly rejected

A sampling plan gives a probability of acceptance at each quality level; at the AQL that probability is high, and lots somewhat worse still have a fair chance of passing. The AQL is not the acceptance number.
std
III.B.1
The probability that a sampling plan rejects a lot whose quality is exactly at the AQL is called:
Producer's risk
Consumer's risk
Average outgoing quality
Lot tolerance percent defective
Rejecting good lots (at the AQL) is the producer's risk, often near 5%. Consumer's risk is accepting lots at a poor quality level such as the LTPD.
std
III.B.1
A sample of 125 units shows 5 defects. Expressed in defects per hundred units, what is the sample result?
5 ÷ 125 × 100 = 4.0 defects per hundred units. Reporting 5.0 ignores the sample size.
std
III.B.2
An inspector samples a lot by taking units from the top layer of each pallet because they are easy to reach. What is the main problem?
The sample size is too small for a lot of that size
The top layer is always the best quality in the lot
Pallets should be inspected 100% instead of sampled
Lower units have no chance of being chosen

Random sampling requires every unit an equal chance of selection, and convenience sampling breaks that, so the result may not represent the lot. Nothing says the top layer is better, only that it may differ.
std
III.B.2
A lot of 2,000 serialized units needs a sample of 50. Which method gives a true random sample?
Take every 40th unit starting with the first serial number
Take the first 50 units packed in the shipping order
Choose 50 serial numbers using a random number generator
Let the operator pick 50 units typical of the lot
Random numbers give every unit an equal, independent chance. A fixed every-40th pattern with no random start is systematic and can line up with cycles in the process.
std
III.B.2
A lot was molded on a four-cavity tool, and parts from all cavities are mixed in each box. Which sampling approach best protects against a problem in one cavity?
Take every unit from whichever box is easiest to open
Randomly select an equal share of units from each cavity
Pick units from the first box packed in the run
Sample units from one cavity, since all four cavities match
Splitting the lot by cavity and sampling randomly within each (stratified random sampling) ensures every cavity is represented. Sampling one cavity assumes away the very difference that matters.
std
III.B.3
A supplier wants to combine parts made on two machines, on two shifts, from two material heats into one inspection lot. What is the best response?
Combine them, but double the sample size to be safe
Accept the request if the supplier signs a certificate
Form lots from product made under the same conditions
Combine them, because a larger lot needs a smaller sample
Lots should be homogeneous so that a sample represents the lot and a decision applies to all of it. Mixing sources hides problems from one source and can reject good product with bad.
std
III.B.3
Why do standard attribute plans not take a fixed percentage of each lot as the sample?
Standards set sample size only by the AQL that is chosen
Protection depends mainly on sample size, not the fraction sampled
A fixed percentage sample cannot be selected at random
Fixed percentages make the sample size too small for large lots

The OC curve is driven mostly by n and the acceptance number, so a 10% sample of a small lot gives far less protection than 10% of a large lot. Sample size in standard plans does grow with lot size, but not proportionally.
std
III.B.3
For the same lot size and AQL, an inspector moves from general inspection level II to level III. What changes?
The acceptance number rises but the sample is unchanged
The AQL is tightened to the next lower value
The sample gets smaller and the risks stay the same
A larger sample and better discrimination
Higher inspection levels give larger samples for the same lot size, which steepens the OC curve. The AQL itself is not changed by the inspection level.
std
III.B.4
A plan calls for n = 80, Ac = 2, Re = 3. The sample contains 3 nonconforming units. What is the decision?
Reject the lot
Accept the lot
Remove the 3 units and accept the lot
Take a second sample of 80
The count meets the rejection number of 3, so the lot is rejected. A second sample is part of double sampling, not a single plan.
std
III.B.4
A plan for nonconforming units is n = 50, Ac = 1, Re = 2. One sampled unit has two defects and the rest have none. What is the decision?
Accept, since only one unit is nonconforming
Reject, since any unit with two defects is critical
Take another sample to settle the count
Reject, since two defects reach the Re of 2
The plan counts nonconforming units, and a unit with two defects is still one nonconforming unit, so the lot is accepted. Counting defects would only be right for a defects-per-hundred-units plan.
std
III.B.4
A customer requires an Ac = 0 sampling plan. What does this mean for the inspector?
Every unit in the lot must be inspected for defects
The lot is proven to contain no nonconforming units
Any nonconforming unit in the sample rejects the lot
The sample size must equal the square root of the lot
With an acceptance number of zero, one nonconforming unit in the sample fails the lot. A clean sample still does not prove the whole lot is defect-free.
std
III.B.5
A double sampling plan is n1 = 32, Ac1 = 0, Re1 = 3; n2 = 32, Ac2 = 3, Re2 = 4. The first sample has 2 nonconforming units and the second has 1. What is the decision?
Reject, since 2 in the first sample exceeds Ac1
Accept, since the combined count of 3 meets Ac2
Take a third sample, since neither limit was clear
Reject, since the combined count of 3 reaches Re1
Two falls between Ac1 and Re1, so a second sample is taken; the cumulative 3 is at Ac2 and the lot is accepted. Exceeding Ac1 alone only triggers the second sample.
std
III.B.5
What is the main advantage of double sampling over single sampling with similar protection?
A smaller producer's risk for every lot that is submitted
No need for an acceptance number on either sample
Simpler records and easier training for all inspectors
A smaller average sample for very good or bad lots
Clearly good or clearly bad lots are often decided on the first, smaller sample, which lowers average sample size. It is more complex to run, not simpler.
std
III.B.5
A single sampling plan has n = 20 and Ac = 0. What is the probability of accepting a lot that is 2% nonconforming?
About 0.40
About 0.60
About 0.67
About 0.98
Pa = 0.98²⁰ ≈ 0.668. About 0.60 comes from the shortcut 1 − 20 × 0.02, which overstates the risk.
std
III.B.5
A single sampling plan has n = 50 and Ac = 1. Using the binomial distribution, what is the probability of accepting a lot that is 2% nonconforming?
About 0.36
About 0.50
About 0.74
About 0.98
std
III.B.5
Two plans both have the acceptance number at about 2% of the sample size. Plan X uses n = 50 and plan Y uses n = 200. How do their OC curves compare?
The curves are the same because the ratio of c to n matches
Y's curve is steeper and discriminates better
Y's curve is flatter because it rejects more good lots
X's curve is steeper because it uses the smaller sample
Larger samples with proportional acceptance numbers move the OC curve toward the ideal vertical line. Keeping the same c/n ratio does not keep the same discrimination.
std
III.B.5
A characteristic is measured on a continuous scale, but its distribution is strongly skewed. Which plan type is the safer choice?
An attributes plan judging each unit as conforming or not
A variables plan using the sample range instead of sigma
A variables plan with the skewed data treated as normal
A variables plan, because it always needs a smaller sample

Variables plans such as Z1.9 rest on a normality assumption, so strong skew makes their estimates of percent nonconforming unreliable. Their smaller sample is only an advantage when the assumption holds.
std
III.B.5
Compared with an attributes plan, what is the main benefit of a variables sampling plan?
Easier inspector training and record keeping
A single plan covers many characteristics
Similar protection from a smaller sample
No assumption about the data's distribution

Measured values carry more information than pass/fail results, so a variables plan needs fewer units for similar protection. It does assume a distribution, usually normal, and needs a separate plan for each characteristic.
std
III.B.5
Under normal inspection with a standard attribute plan, two of the last five consecutive lots have been rejected. What should happen next?
Switch to reduced inspection
Stop inspection until the supplier responds
Stay on normal inspection
Switch to tightened inspection

The standard switching rule moves normal to tightened when two of five or fewer consecutive lots are rejected on original inspection. Reduced inspection is earned by sustained good results, not by rejections.
std
III.B.5
A supplier is on tightened inspection. Under standard switching rules, what returns it to normal inspection?
Five consecutive lots accepted on tightened inspection
Ten lots in a row accepted with no nonconforming units
A corrective action plan accepted by the buyer's quality team
One lot accepted under tightened inspection, with no defects
The return from tightened to normal requires five consecutive accepted lots under tightened inspection. A corrective action plan alone does not show that quality has recovered.

III.C.1
Porosity in purchased castings is found only after machining and assembly. Which inspection point would have caught it at the lowest cost?
First-article inspection
Final inspection
In-process inspection
Incoming inspection
Incoming inspection checks purchased material before value is added, so defects found there cost least. First-article inspection proves a new setup, not every arriving lot of castings.

III.C.1
A machine shop changes to a new fixture for a part it has made for years. What inspection should take place before the run continues?
Incoming inspection of the raw bar stock
First-piece inspection of the new setup
Final inspection of the completed lot only
No inspection, since the part design is unchanged
A new fixture changes the process, so the first parts should be verified before production continues. Waiting for final inspection risks a full lot of bad parts.

III.C.1
What most distinguishes a full first-article inspection from routine in-process checks?
It checks only critical features at set time intervals
It is done by the operator instead of an inspector
It verifies every drawing characteristic on the first part
It is done only after customer complaints arise
A first-article inspection checks all characteristics to prove that the process can make the part as designed. In-process checks sample selected characteristics during the run.
std
III.C.1
On a 5,000-piece run, a cutting tool wears gradually and the bore drifts oversize. Which inspection best limits the number of bad parts made?
A first-piece inspection before the run begins
Incoming inspection of the bar stock before the run
Final inspection of the finished lot after the run
In-process checks at set intervals during the run
Periodic in-process checks detect drift while the run is underway so it can be corrected. The first piece was good, so a first-piece check cannot catch wear that comes later.
std
III.C.1
A final inspector finds that the in-process inspection record for a lot is missing. What should he do?
Hold the lot until the gap is resolved
Release the lot if his final checks pass
Scrap the lot because the record is missing
Release the lot and note the gap in the log

Final inspection confirms that all required inspections and records are complete before release. Passing final checks does not cover characteristics only checked in process; scrapping is premature without evidence.
std
III.C.1
Which inspection is the last chance to confirm that finished product meets all requirements before it ships?
Incoming inspection
Final inspection
First-piece inspection
In-process inspection

Final inspection verifies the completed product and its records before release to the customer. In-process inspection happens during manufacture, before later operations that could still create defects.
std
III.C.2
An inspector knows which operator made each lot and tends to pass borderline parts from the most experienced operator. Which control addresses this error best?
Recalibrate the gauges used for borderline parts
Add a second shift of inspectors to share the load
Remove source information so inspection is done blind
Schedule more frequent rest breaks for the inspector
This is inspector bias, and hiding the source removes what drives it. Breaks address fatigue and calibration addresses gauge error, not expectations.
std
III.C.2
Visual inspectors on a 10-hour shift miss many more surface defects in the last two hours. What is the most likely cause and best response?
Fatigue; rotate tasks and schedule regular breaks
Distraction; move inspection to a separate room
Bias; hide the operator's name from inspectors
Setup error; recheck the lighting fixtures daily
Detection falling off late in long shifts points to fatigue, which task rotation and breaks address. A separate room helps with distraction, which would not be tied to the end of the shift.
std
III.C.2
A histogram of recorded diameters shows a pile-up of readings just inside the upper limit and almost none just above it. What does this most likely indicate?
Fatigue from too many parts measured per hour
Flinching: borderline readings recorded as in tolerance
A gauge with too little resolution for the tolerance
Normal variation for a process centered near the limit
A cliff at the limit with readings stacked just inside is the classic sign of flinching, giving borderline parts the benefit of the doubt. Normal variation would tail off smoothly across the limit.
std
III.C.2
An inspector counting defects on a panel is interrupted three times by phone calls and loses her place. Which error source is this, and what is the best fix?
Setup error; recheck the panel fixture each time
Fatigue; shorten her shift and add rest periods
Distraction; remove the interruptions
Bias; have a second inspector repeat every count
Interruptions that break concentration are distraction, best handled by removing them from the inspection area. Re-counting everything treats the symptom and doubles the workload.
std
III.C.2
To clear a backlog before shift end, an inspector skips the second check on each part and signs off the lots. What is the root problem, and what should he have done?
Distraction; move to a quieter inspection area
Flinching; record the borderline parts separately
Fatigue; take a break and then finish the checks
Poor time management; escalate the backlog
Rushing to meet a time pressure and cutting required steps is poor time management, and the right move is to raise the capacity issue. Taking a break does not deal with the pressure to skip steps.
std
III.C.2
Every height gauge reading on a shift is 0.02 mm higher than the same parts measure on a CMM. The gauge was zeroed on a surface plate with a chip under it. Which error is this?
Fatigue error
Setup error
Flinching error
Cosine error
A consistent offset from zeroing on a contaminated reference is a setup error. Cosine error comes from an indicator angle and grows with the size of the reading, rather than giving a fixed offset.
std
III.C.2
A dial test indicator's stylus is set 20° from the ideal angle to the surface, and it reads 0.050 mm. What is the approximate true displacement?
True ≈ indicated × cos 20° = 0.050 × 0.940 ≈ 0.047 mm. Dividing by the cosine (0.053) corrects in the wrong direction, since cosine error makes the reading too large.
std
III.C.2
The stylus of a lever-type dial test indicator is not set at the correct angle to the direction of movement. How does cosine error affect the reading?
The reading is smaller than the true movement
The reading is unchanged but less repeatable
The reading is larger than the true movement
The reading shifts by a fixed amount, as a zero error would

Misalignment makes the indicator register more travel than actually occurred, so true movement is the reading times the cosine of the angle. The error grows with the reading rather than being a fixed offset.
std
III.C.3
A plant records the cure date on elastomer seals and will not issue seals older than a set age from that date. What is this practice?
Lot numbering
Barcoding
FIFO
Age control
Limiting use by the time since manufacture or cure is age control. FIFO governs the order stock is issued, but by itself does not stop an old seal being used.
std
III.C.3
An epoxy with a 6-month shelf life was made on 14 February. On 1 September a technician wants to use it. What should happen?
Do not issue it; hold it as expired material
Use it, because sealed containers do not expire
Relabel it with a new date and issue it
Use it only on parts marked as noncritical
The shelf life ended around 14 August, so the material is expired and must be held from use. Relabeling or restricting use to noncritical parts bypasses the requirement.
std
III.C.3
Parts that expire are found at the back of a storage rack because new receipts are always placed in front. What change fixes this?
Order smaller quantities from the supplier
Count the rack inventory more frequently
Store the newest receipts on the top shelf
Load from the back and pick from the front
Loading from one end and picking from the other enforces first-in first-out, so older stock is used first. Counting more often finds the problem but does not change the issue order.
std
III.C.3
Shop travelers show several lot numbers with digits transposed when copied by hand at each operation. Which method best prevents this?
Scan a barcode label at each operation
Record lot numbers only at final inspection
Use larger handwriting on the travelers
Have a second clerk retype each entry

Barcode scanning captures the identifier without manual transcription, removing transposition errors. Retyping still relies on manual copying, and recording only at the end loses traceability through the process.
std
III.C.3
A label shows the Julian date code 26045, where 26 is the year. On what date was the item made?
26 April 2026
14 February 2026
15 February 2026
Day 045 of a year is 31 days of January plus 14, which is 14 February. Reading 045 as month and day (4 May) misreads the Julian format.
std
III.C.3
A field failure is traced to one batch of resin. Because each molded lot records the resin batch used, only three lots are recalled. Which traceability method made this possible?
Shelf-life labeling of the stored resin
Lot numbers linked to resin batches
FIFO issue of the finished goods stock
Part numbering on each finished molding
Lot numbers link a group of product to the conditions and materials used, so a recall can be limited to affected lots. A part number identifies the design and is the same for every lot.
std
III.C.3
What is the difference between a part number and a lot number?
They mean the same thing in most traceability systems
Part number: the design; lot number: a production group
A part number identifies a single unit; a lot number the design
A part number changes with each lot produced
The part number stays the same for every unit of a given design and revision, while lot numbers separate groups made under common conditions. A unique single-unit identifier is a serial number.
std
III.C.4
An inspector finds nonconforming brackets on a line-side rack and tags them. Why should they also be moved to a hold area?
Moving the parts formally completes disposition
Tags are not valid evidence for an MRB decision
The rack must be left empty for the auditors
Separation stops use even if the tag falls off
Segregation adds a physical barrier so tagged parts cannot be picked up by mistake. Moving parts to hold is not disposition, which is still decided by the MRB or other authority.
std
III.C.4
A nonconforming two-ton casting is too heavy to move to the hold area. What is the best way to control it?
Leave it untagged until a forklift is free
Mark it with chalk and resume work around it
Tag it where it sits and rope off the area
Record it in the log but do not mark the part
When material cannot be moved, it must still be clearly identified and kept from use, by tagging it and marking off the area. A log entry alone does nothing to warn someone standing at the part.
std
III.C.4
A plant uses green, yellow and red container labels. A bin with a green "accepted" label holds parts named in an open nonconformance report. What should the inspector do?
Relabel it as on hold and segregate the bin
Add a red label beside the existing green label
Leave the label, since the report is still open
Add a note to the report and leave the bin in place
Status labels must match actual status, so the accepted label must be replaced and the parts segregated until disposition. Two conflicting labels on one bin invites mistakes.
std
III.C.4
Small fasteners from a rejected lot are bagged. What is the most effective way to label them?
Note the status on the lot's paperwork only
Label only the outer carton holding the bags
Label each bag with its status and NCR
Label the bag on top and leave the others plain
Each unit of packaging that could be separated must carry its status so no bag can be used by mistake. Labeling only the carton fails as soon as bags are removed.
std
III.C.5
A crack in a brake line fitting could cause loss of braking. How should this defect be classified?
Minor
Cosmetic
Major
Critical
A defect likely to cause hazardous or unsafe conditions for users is critical. A major defect affects function or usability without that safety hazard.

III.C.5
A bent connector pin stops a control module from working but creates no safety hazard. How should this defect be classified?
Minor
Major
Critical
Incidental
A defect that is likely to cause failure or greatly reduce usability, without creating a hazard, is major. Critical is kept for defects that create unsafe conditions.
std
III.C.5
A small scratch on the inside of a housing cover, not visible in use, has no effect on function. How should this defect be classified?
Minor
Major
Critical
Functional
A minor defect departs from standards but does not materially reduce usability or function. Calling it major would overstate its effect.
std
III.C.5
A sampling plan sets AQL values by defect class. How should critical, major and minor AQLs compare?
All three the same, since the AQL is a single value
Minor lowest, then major, with critical highest
Critical lowest, then major, with minor highest
Major lowest, with critical and minor equal
More severe classes get stricter (lower) AQLs or 100% inspection, so fewer of those defects are tolerated. Using one AQL for every class ignores the difference in consequences.

III.C.6
Shafts ground slightly oversize are reground until they are within drawing limits. What disposition is this?
Rework
Repair
Customer waiver
Use as is
Rework brings a nonconforming product into full conformance with requirements. Repair makes it acceptable for use while it still does not meet the original requirement.
