III.C.6
Which disposition sends product back through the original or an alternate process step, such as re-plating or re-heat-treating?
Scrap
Customer waiver
Reinspect
Reprocess
Reprocessing repeats or substitutes a process step to correct the product, followed by inspection of the affected characteristics. Reinspection only checks the product again without changing it.
std
III.C.6
A lot was rejected on a bore gauge that was later found out of calibration. Which disposition is most appropriate?
Scrap the entire lot right away
Reinspect with a calibrated gauge
Rework every bore to the low limit
Request a customer waiver for the lot
The rejection itself is in doubt, so reinspecting with a good gauge establishes the true status. Scrapping or reworking parts that may conform wastes good product.
std
III.C.6
The MRB orders a lot of cracked castings scrapped. What should happen to the castings next?
Return them to stock with a red tag on the box
Sell them as seconds to a commercial customer
Mark or mutilate them so they cannot re-enter use
Store them in the hold area until the next audit
Scrapped product should be made unusable so it cannot be mistakenly or deliberately put back into production. Keeping them tagged in stock still leaves a path back into use.
std
III.C.6
The MRB decides that out-of-print parts will work, but the drawing is the customer's design. What is needed before shipment?
A written waiver (concession) from the customer
An MRB record showing the parts were reworked
A note on the packing list describing the issue
A signature from the plant's production manager
When the customer owns the requirement, only the customer can authorize use of nonconforming product. Internal signatures cannot waive another party's requirement.
std
III.C.6
How does a customer waiver (concession) differ from a deviation permit?
A waiver is internal; a deviation always comes from the customer
A waiver is granted after the fact; a deviation before
A waiver is approved before production; a deviation after it
A waiver is permanent; a deviation changes the drawing

A concession or waiver authorizes use or release of product already found nonconforming, while a deviation permit is granted in advance for a limited quantity or time. Neither changes the drawing permanently.
std
III.C.6
A production supervisor asks an inspector to release a batch that is slightly out of tolerance because the customer is waiting. What should the inspector do?
Release it if the supervisor signs for it
Release it with a note on the shipping papers
Scrap it so it cannot cause any delay
Keep it on hold and refer it to the MRB

Disposition of nonconforming product belongs to the MRB or other designated authority, not to the inspector or supervisor. Scrapping is also a disposition the inspector has no authority to make alone.
std
III.D.1
Which method is best for finding internal gas porosity in an aluminum casting and providing a permanent image record?
Dye penetrant testing
Magnetic particle
Visual examination
Radiography (X-ray)
Radiography shows internal voids as density differences and produces a film or digital image. Penetrant only finds defects open to the surface, and magnetic particle cannot be used on aluminum.
std
III.D.1
An automated line needs fast, noncontact checks of copper tubing for surface cracks. Which method fits best?
Magnetic particle
Dye penetrant
Eddy current
Radiography
Eddy current works on conductive materials, needs no couplant or contact and suits high-speed tube lines. Magnetic particle needs ferromagnetic material, which copper is not.
std
III.D.1
A buyer needs to find laminations deep inside 50 mm steel plate. Which method is most suitable?
Eddy current
Ultrasonic testing
Dye penetrant
Visual examination
Ultrasonic waves pass through thick sections and reflect from internal planar flaws such as laminations. Eddy current is limited to the surface and near-surface region.
std
III.D.1
Which flaw cannot be detected by dye penetrant testing?
A fully enclosed internal void
A lap open at the part's surface
Surface porosity on a machined face
A fine crack open to the surface
Penetrant must seep into an opening, so it only reveals surface-breaking discontinuities. Fine surface cracks are exactly what it is best at finding.
std
III.D.1
A weld on austenitic stainless steel must be checked for surface cracks. Why is magnetic particle testing unsuitable?
The test needs a radiation-safe area
The test finds only internal defects
The steel is not ferromagnetic
The weld surface is too smooth
Magnetic particle testing needs a ferromagnetic part to carry the magnetic field, and austenitic stainless steel is essentially nonmagnetic. Penetrant testing would be the usual choice.
std
III.D.1
Which inspection method allows burrs inside a drilled hydraulic manifold passage to be seen without cutting the part?
Brinell hardness testing of the block
A borescope (optical inspection)
Magnetic particle testing of the passages
Drop testing of the assembled manifold
A borescope is an optical aid that lets the inspector view internal passages directly. Magnetic particle testing reveals cracks, not burrs, and drop and hardness tests do not show internal geometry.
std
III.D.1
Before running dye penetrant on a weld, what NDT step should come first?
Visual examination of the weld
Radiography of the weld
A tensile test on the weld
Ultrasonic testing of the weld
Visual examination is the cheapest NDT method and finds obvious defects and surface conditions that affect later tests. A tensile test is destructive and is not a step before penetrant.
std
III.D.1
Inspectors compare the outline of a stamped gear on a 20× projector screen with a chart overlay of the tolerance band. What method is this?
Radiographic testing
Ultrasonic testing
Eddy current testing
Profile inspection
Projecting a part's outline and comparing it with a toleranced overlay is profile inspection on an optical comparator. The other methods look for flaws, not outline shape.
std
III.D.1
What is the main advantage of nondestructive testing over destructive testing?
It measures strength values directly in physical units
The part survives, so all parts can be tested
It requires no trained or certified personnel at all
It works the same way on every material and shape
Because NDT leaves the part intact, it can be applied to 100% of production. Strength values such as tensile strength come from destructive tests.
std
III.D.2
A Ø10 mm steel test bar breaks at a maximum load of 31,400 N. What is its approximate tensile strength?
About 100 MPa
About 400 MPa
About 1,000 MPa
About 3,140 MPa
Area = π × 5² ≈ 78.5 mm², and 31,400 ÷ 78.5 ≈ 400 MPa. About 100 MPa comes from using π × 10², treating the diameter as the radius.
std
III.D.2
A tensile specimen has a 50 mm gauge length before testing. After fracture, the pieces fitted together measure 62 mm. What is the percent elongation?
Elongation = (62 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = 24%. 19% divides by the final length instead of the original.
std
III.D.2
On a tensile test, which property marks the stress at which the material begins to deform permanently?
Modulus of elasticity
Ultimate tensile strength
Percent elongation
Yield strength
Yield strength is where elastic behavior ends and permanent deformation begins. Ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress reached, later in the test.
std
III.D.2
Five crimped terminals are pulled apart to a minimum 90 N specification. Results are 112, 105, 88, 120 and 97 N. What is the correct conclusion?
The test must be repeated on the same five terminals
The sample fails, because one terminal is below 90 N
The sample passes, because the average is above 90 N
The sample passes, because four of five are above 90 N
A minimum force requirement applies to each piece, and 88 N is below it. The 104.4 N average hides the low unit, and the destroyed terminals cannot be retested.
std
III.D.2
A packaged product passes a drop test in the lab, but a repeat test by the customer fails. Which factors must be fixed for the results to be comparable?
Drop height, impact orientation and impact surface
The time of day and the number of people present
The weight of the product only, as other factors cancel
Box color, label position and the outer carton print

Drop test severity depends on height, which face, edge or corner strikes, and what it strikes, so these must be set in the test method. Product weight matters but does not make the other factors cancel.
std
III.D.3
A technician applies 40 N at the end of a wrench, 0.25 m from the bolt center, at right angles to the handle. What torque is applied?
10 N·m
40 N·m
Torque = force × arm = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N·m. 160 N·m comes from dividing force by the arm length instead of multiplying.
std
III.D.3
Two lots of identical bolts are tightened to the same torque, but one lot is lubricated. How does clamp load compare?
The same in both lots, since torque sets the clamp load
Lower in the lubricated lot, since the threads slip under load
Higher in the lubricated lot, since less is lost to friction
Higher in the dry lot, since friction adds to the tension
Most applied torque is spent overcoming friction, so less friction leaves more to stretch the bolt and raise clamp load. Torque is only an indirect measure of clamp load.
std
III.D.3
A pressure-decay leak test allows a maximum drop of 1.0 kPa per minute. A part loses 0.6 kPa in a 30-second test. What is the result?
Pass, at a rate of 0.3 kPa per minute
Fail, at a rate of 1.8 kPa per minute
Pass, at a rate of 0.6 kPa per minute
Fail, at a rate of 1.2 kPa per minute
0.6 kPa in 30 s equals 1.2 kPa per minute, which exceeds the 1.0 limit. Reading 0.6 as the per-minute rate ignores that the test lasted only half a minute.
std
III.D.3
Which leak test method can detect the smallest leaks?
Helium mass spectrometer testing
Soap solution testing at the joints
Bubble immersion testing in water
Pressure decay testing with air

A helium mass spectrometer detects trace amounts of helium and finds far smaller leaks than other common methods. Pressure decay is limited by the part's volume and the resolution of the pressure reading.
std
III.D.3
Each lifting hook gets a proof-load test at a set load and is checked for no permanent deformation. How does this differ from a tensile test?
It measures elongation after fracture on a test specimen
It pulls the hook until it breaks and records the peak load
It loads below failure and the hook stays in use
It checks hardness at the hook's throat before loading
A functional tension (proof) test loads each part to a specified level to confirm it performs, leaving it usable. A tensile test pulls a specimen to fracture and destroys it.
std
III.D.3
A compression spring deflects 15 mm under a 120 N load. What is its spring rate?
8 N/mm
135 N/mm
Rate = load ÷ deflection = 120 ÷ 15 = 8 N/mm. 0.125 is the inverse, deflection per newton.
std
III.D.3
Shipping cartons will be stacked six high in a warehouse. Which test best confirms they will not collapse?
Drop testing
Compression testing
Leak testing
Torque testing
Stacking applies a steady vertical load, which a box compression test simulates. A drop test checks impact during handling, not sustained stacking load.
std
III.D.4
Why is Brinell testing well suited to coarse-grained iron castings?
It reads directly in Rockwell C hardness units
The large indent averages the structure
It needs no surface preparation of any kind
Its small indent can target one grain at a time
The large ball and load make a wide impression that averages over the heterogeneous structure. A small indent would give scattered readings depending on where it lands.
std
III.D.4
An inspector tests a hardened tool steel part at about 60 on the Rockwell C scale. Why is the Rockwell B scale wrong for it?
The B scale uses a diamond cone meant for thin coatings
The B scale gives the same number on any hardened steel
B uses a ball and lower load, for softer metals
The B scale is meant only for rubber and plastic parts
Rockwell B uses a 1/16 in ball at 100 kgf for softer metals such as brass and annealed steel; hardened steel needs the diamond-cone C scale. Rubber and plastics use durometer scales.
std
III.D.4
A Rockwell C test on thin sheet leaves a visible mark on the underside. What should the inspector do?
Discard it and retest on a lighter-load scale
Average it with a reading taken from the underside
Accept the reading, since the indent was on the top side
Add a correction factor for the sheet's thickness
A mark on the back shows the sample was too thin for the load, so the anvil influenced the reading. A superficial scale or a micro-hardness method uses lighter loads suited to thin material.
std
III.D.4
Which instrument should be used to check the hardness of 70-hardness rubber O-rings?
A Knoop micro-hardness tester
A Rockwell C tester
A Brinell tester
A Shore A durometer
Shore A durometers measure soft elastomers such as O-ring rubber. Rockwell and Brinell are for metals and would not give meaningful results on rubber.
std
III.D.4
A lab needs a hardness profile through a 0.3 mm carburized case on a sectioned gear tooth. Which method fits?
Micro-hardness testing (Vickers or Knoop)
Rockwell B testing across the tooth flank surface
Shore D durometer testing
Brinell testing with a 10 mm ball
Micro-hardness uses very light loads and small indents, so readings can be spaced across a thin case. A 10 mm Brinell ball is far larger than the case depth.
std
III.D.4
A drawing calls for 30–35 HRC. The lab tested in Brinell and converted the result to HRC with a table. How should the inspector view this?
Any hardness scale meets the drawing as long as it passes
Conversions are approximate; test on the specified scale
Conversions are exact, so the result is fully valid
Brinell is more precise, so it should be preferred
Hardness conversions are empirical and material dependent, so they only approximate the specified scale. When the drawing specifies HRC, the test should be on HRC.
std
III.E
Operators can edit the accept limits in an automated test stand's program. Which control safeguards the software best?
Post a sign asking operators not to change the program limits
Have the stand rerun each test twice to confirm the result
Restrict edits to authorized users under version control
Print the program limits and file them in the quality office
Safeguarding prevents unauthorized change, through access control and version tracking. A sign or printed copy does not stop anyone from editing the program.
std
III.E
At the start of each shift, a vision system is run with master parts holding known good and known bad features. What is this?
A comparison of test results
A calibration interval study
An installation qualification
A functional check
Running known masters confirms the system detects what it should before production use. An installation qualification is done once when the system is installed, not every shift.
std
III.E
A new leak test stand runs 30 parts that were already tested on the validated old stand, and the two sets of results are reviewed side by side. What technique is this?
Parameter identification
Comparison of test results
A shift-start functional check
Safeguarding of software
Testing the same parts on both systems and comparing the outcomes shows whether the new software gives equivalent results. A functional check uses known masters rather than a second system.
std
III.E
Before validating test software, a team lists its inputs, outputs, units, test limits and settings. Which basic tool is this?
Identification of attributes and parameters
A shift-start functional check of the test stand
Safeguarding of the software against change
Comparison of results with another stand
Knowing exactly which parameters and attributes the software handles defines what must be validated and controlled. Comparison of results comes later, once the test cases are defined.
std
III.E
A vendor issues an update to the software in a CMM. What should happen before the CMM is used for acceptance?
Keep using the old version until it stops working
Install it and check results at the next calibration date
Revalidate the software, at least with regression test cases
Install it, since vendor updates are always pre-validated

Any change to validated software can affect results, so it must be revalidated before acceptance use, typically by rerunning test cases with known answers. Waiting for the next calibration lets unverified results be used in the meantime.
std
III.E
Which software validation method runs the program on input data whose correct outputs are already known?
Checking that the license key is valid
Reviewing the vendor's user manual
Surveying operators about the results
Testing with known test cases
Feeding inputs with known correct answers and comparing outputs directly shows whether the software calculates correctly. Reading the manual says what it should do, not whether it does.
std
III.E
In an IQ/OQ/PQ validation approach, which stage confirms that test software works correctly across its specified operating range?
Installation qualification (IQ)
Design qualification (DQ)
Operational qualification (OQ)
Performance qualification (PQ)
OQ challenges the system across its operating ranges, including limits. IQ confirms correct installation, and PQ confirms consistent performance in actual production use.
std
IV.A.1
One plant adds 100% final inspection to catch cracked housings. Another changes its molding settings so the cracks no longer form. How do the two approaches differ?
The first is prevention, because it stops defects before they are shipped
Both are prevention, since neither lets cracked housings reach the customer
The first detects defects after they occur; the second prevents them
The second is detection, because it relies on watching the molding process
Inspection finds defects that have already been made, while changing the process stops them from being made. Keeping bad parts from shipping is still detection, not prevention.
std
IV.A.1
In one month a shop records: scrap $12,000; rework $8,000; re-inspection of reworked parts $2,000; receiving inspection $6,000; warranty repairs $15,000. What is the internal failure cost?

Internal failure costs arise before delivery: scrap, rework and re-inspection of reworked parts, $12,000 + $8,000 + $2,000 = $22,000. Receiving inspection is an appraisal cost and warranty is external failure, so adding either overstates the figure.
std
IV.A.1
A plant manager says the plant's cost of poor quality is low because its inspection budget is small. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
Most poor-quality cost comes from failures such as scrap, rework and warranty
The inspection budget should be compared with sales instead of other costs
Cost of poor quality counts only costs the customer reports after delivery
Inspection costs are prevention costs and are left out of quality cost reports

The cost of poor quality is driven mainly by internal and external failures, which a small inspection budget says nothing about. Inspection is an appraisal cost, not a prevention cost, and internal failures count as well as those found by customers.
std
IV.A.1
Annual scrap cost at a plant fell from $40,000 to $30,000 after an improvement project. What is the percent change?
Percent change is (new − original) / original × 100 = (30,000 − 40,000) / 40,000 × 100 = −25%. Dividing by the new value gives −33.3%, and dropping the sign hides that cost went down.
std
IV.A.1
Which description best fits total quality management (TQM)?
A program run by the quality department to inspect all product before it is shipped
An organization-wide approach in which everyone improves processes to meet customer needs
A statistical method for setting control limits on the key outputs of a process
A certification scheme in which a registrar audits the company against a published standard

TQM involves every function and level in continual process improvement aimed at customer satisfaction. Making quality the job of an inspection department is the opposite of TQM's shared responsibility.
std
IV.A.1
A supplier's parts meet every drawing requirement, yet its largest customer is moving business to a competitor because of late deliveries and slow replies. What does this show?
Delivery and service fall outside the scope of quality management
The supplier should tighten its tolerances to win the business back
Meeting specifications alone does not ensure customer satisfaction
The complaints are invalid, since the parts meet all drawing requirements
Customers judge the whole experience, including delivery and responsiveness, not just conformance. Tighter tolerances would add cost without touching the reasons the customer is leaving.
std
IV.A.2
Which of the following is a process rather than a product?
A hardened steel shaft ready for assembly
A box of 500 machined steel brackets
Heat treating shafts for hardness
A calibration certificate for a micrometer
A process is a set of activities that turns inputs into outputs; heat treating is such an activity. The shaft, the brackets and even the certificate are outputs of processes, so they are products.
std
IV.A.2
A heat treat furnace runs cold for one shift. The parts pass dimensional inspection but later fail fatigue testing. What does this illustrate?
Fatigue failures come from product design rather than processing conditions
One process step can change product properties that later checks do not catch
Dimensional inspection is enough to verify the effect of heat treatment
Furnace drift matters only when the parts also fail dimensional checks

Heat treatment sets material properties that a dimensional check cannot see, so a single bad step reached the final product unnoticed. Passing dimensional inspection says nothing about hardness or fatigue life.
std
IV.A.2
A part goes through three steps with first-pass yields of 98%, 95% and 99%. What is the rolled throughput yield?
Rolled throughput yield is the product of the step yields: 0.98 × 0.95 × 0.99 = 0.922. Averaging the yields (97.3%) or taking the worst step (95.0%) ignores how losses at each step compound.
std
IV.A.2
Design engineering changes a welded bracket from steel to aluminum to save weight, but the welding process is not reviewed. What is the most likely result?
Final inspection will catch any problem, so the process can stay the same
The final product is unaffected because only the material has changed
Weld settings developed for steel may give defective joints in aluminum
Only the drawing revision needs updating, since processes follow drawings
Design, material and process are linked, and a material change usually requires the process to change with it. Relying on final inspection treats the symptom and may miss internal weld defects.
std
IV.A.2
A designer specifies a tolerance tighter than the existing machining process can hold. What is the most likely result if nothing else changes?
No effect, because the machine adjusts itself to the drawing tolerance
Better capability indices, because tighter limits improve Cp and Cpk
More scrap and sorting until the process or the design is changed
Fewer defects, because tighter limits push operators to work harder
When the design asks for more than the process can deliver, more output falls outside the limits and must be sorted or scrapped. Tighter limits actually lower Cp and Cpk for the same process spread.
std
IV.B.1
A company uses its own trained auditors to check its quality system at its own plant. This is:
An internal (first-party) audit
A second-party audit
An external registration audit
A third-party certification audit
An organization auditing itself is an internal, or first-party, audit. Second- and third-party audits are external: done by a customer or by an independent body.
std
IV.B.1
A customer's quality engineer visits a supplier to audit the controls on the parts the customer buys. What kind of audit is this?
An external, second-party audit
An internal, first-party audit
A self-assessment by the supplier
A third-party certification audit
A customer auditing its supplier is a second-party audit, which is external to the supplier. A third-party audit is done by an independent body such as a registrar.
std
IV.B.1
An audit checks whether the organization's whole management system, including its policies, processes and how they link, meets ISO 9001. This is a:
System audit
Process audit
Calibration audit
Product audit
A system audit looks at the management system as a whole against a standard. Product and process audits look at one output or one process, not the full system.
std
IV.B.1
An auditor pulls packed units from the shipping dock and checks them against the drawing and packaging requirements. This is a:
System audit
Second-party audit
Product audit
Process audit
A product audit examines finished output to confirm it meets requirements. A process audit would instead look at how the work is done, such as settings, methods and training.
std
IV.B.1
An auditor watches a soldering operation and checks that the settings, operator training and equipment match the documented method. This is a:
Process audit
System audit
Product audit
Third-party audit
A process audit checks how one process is run against its requirements. A product audit would check the soldered assemblies themselves rather than the way they are made.
std
IV.B.2
Before an audit the lead auditor writes that it will cover receiving inspection and stores at one plant, to check conformance to the incoming inspection procedure. This statement sets the audit's:
Findings and conclusions
Follow-up and closure
Schedule and resources
Scope and purpose
Scope is what the audit covers (areas, site) and purpose is why it is done (check conformance to a procedure). Schedule and resources say when and with whom, which this statement does not address.
std
IV.B.2
An audit of a large plant that runs three shifts is planned for one auditor for half a day. What is the main planning concern?
Each shift should be audited against a different standard to save time
The auditee should not be told of the audit until the auditor arrives
Audits must use a team of at least three auditors to be considered valid by a registrar
The time and people may be too few to cover the scope, including all shifts
Planning must match resources and time to the scope; half a day cannot fairly sample three shifts of a large plant. There is no fixed minimum team size, and audits are normally announced.
std
IV.B.2
What is the main purpose of the opening meeting of an audit?
Interview the operators whose work will be sampled during the audit
Present early findings so the auditee can begin corrective action at once
Confirm the scope, plan and logistics and explain how the audit will run
Agree with the auditee which nonconformities will appear in the report
The opening meeting confirms the plan and arrangements with the auditee and sets expectations. Findings come later, and they are based on evidence, not negotiated.
std
IV.B.2
During an interview an operator gives a vague answer about how she sets up a press. What should the auditor do next?
Ask her to show how she does the setup
Ask her supervisor to answer for her to save audit time
Read her the procedure and ask whether she agrees with it
Record a nonconformity, since she could not explain her job clearly
Asking the person to demonstrate turns a vague answer into objective evidence. A nonconformity needs evidence that a requirement was not met, and a poor explanation alone is not that evidence.
std
IV.B.2
An auditor reads the calibration procedure and then pulls ten calibration records for gauges in use on the floor. Why look at both?
The procedure alone is enough once it has been formally approved
The records show what should happen and the procedure shows what did
The procedure shows what should happen and the records show what did
Records need checking only when the procedure is out of date
Documents state the planned arrangements; records are evidence of what was actually done. An approved procedure shows intent but not that it is followed.
std
IV.B.2
After fieldwork, the audit team sees the same missing-approval problem in four departments. What does analysis of the results most likely support?
Reporting it only for the department where it was seen first
One finding on a system-wide weakness in the approval process
Rewriting the procedure now so it is closed before the report
Dropping the issue since each department had only one case
A pattern across departments points to a system cause, which is more useful to report than scattered single cases. Auditors report evidence; they do not fix the process during the audit.
std
IV.B.2
At the closing meeting the auditee disagrees with a finding. What is the best approach?
Tell the auditee that findings cannot be discussed at this stage
Delay the closing meeting until the auditee accepts every finding
Review the evidence together and record any disagreement that remains
Withdraw the finding so that the closing meeting can end on full agreement
Findings rest on objective evidence, which should be reviewed openly; if a difference of opinion remains, it is noted. Dropping a supported finding just to keep the peace weakens the audit.
std
IV.B.2
Which content belongs in a formal audit report?
The auditor's personal views on staff, not tied to evidence
Names of the operators who made errors so they can be disciplined
Scope, criteria, findings with their evidence, and conclusions
Proposed staffing changes the auditor thinks the area needs
An audit report states what was audited, against what, what was found with evidence, and the conclusions. Reports address the system, not blame of individuals or unsupported opinion.
std
IV.B.2
Why are audit plans, notes, reports and CAR records kept after an audit is closed?
To let the auditee reopen findings whenever later results improve
To show the program was carried out and support follow-up and trends
Because the auditee owns the notes and must hold the originals
To remove the need to send a written report to management after each audit
Retained audit records are evidence that the program was carried out and let later audits and reviews follow up and spot trends. They do not replace the report to management.
std
IV.B.2
A department reports that its corrective action for a calibration finding is complete. What should the audit function do?
Open a new CAR at once in case the original action proves not to be enough
Close the CAR on the department's word, since it owns the process
Verify with objective evidence that the action was done and is effective
Leave the area alone until the next scheduled annual audit
Closure needs evidence that the action was taken and that it worked. Accepting the department's statement alone leaves the loop open.
std
IV.B.3
What is the main purpose of an audit checklist?
To replace the need to collect objective evidence during the audit
To limit the auditor to questions written before the audit began
To help cover key requirements and record evidence consistently
To give the auditee the questions so answers can be prepared
A checklist is a guide that helps the auditor cover the requirements and record evidence. It should not stop the auditor from following up on what is found.
std
IV.B.3
During an audit, an auditor keeps a running sheet of each sample taken, where it came from and when it was checked. This is a:
Audit plan
Checklist
Corrective action request
Log sheet
A log sheet is a running record of what was examined and when. A checklist lists what to look for, not a record of each sample taken.
std
IV.B.3
An auditor plans to check 20 of 400 travelers, picked at random across all shifts and months. Why use random selection?
Random selection makes sure every nonconformity in the population is found
It removes the need to define the population before sampling
It lets the auditee choose the records that best show the process
Every record has a chance of selection, so the sample is representative
Random selection gives each item a known chance of being chosen, so the sample fairly represents the whole. No sample can find every nonconformity.
std
IV.B.3
An audit sampling plan calls for n = 50 records, Ac = 1, Re = 2. The auditor finds 2 records missing a required signature. What is the result?
Reject, since 2 equals Re
Accept, because 2 in 50 is under 5 percent
Accept, because only one more than Ac was found
Take a second sample of 50 before deciding
With Ac = 1 and Re = 2, finding 2 nonconforming records means rejection. A single sampling plan does not allow a second sample, and the decision follows the plan numbers, not a percent rule.
std
IV.B.3
Which activity is a record review?
Watching an inspector measure parts at the receiving dock
Interviewing a buyer about how new suppliers are selected
Checking completed inspection reports for results, signatures and dates
Checking that the current procedure covers each clause of the applicable standard
Records are evidence of activities performed, so reviewing completed reports is a record review. Comparing a procedure with the standard is a document review.
std
IV.B.3
Before going on site, an auditor compares the auditee's procedures with the requirements of the standard. This is:
Forward tracing of orders
Product audit of samples
Document review
Record review of results
A document review checks that the planned arrangements, such as procedures, meet the criteria. A record review would look at evidence of work done, which this is not.
std
IV.B.3
An auditor starts with a customer order and follows it through planning, production, inspection and shipping. This is:
Random sampling
Forward tracing
Document review
Backward tracing
Forward tracing follows work from the start of a process to its end. Backward tracing begins with an output and works back to its sources.
std
IV.B.3

To analyze a failure only after it has already reached the customer

FMEA is a proactive method for anticipating failures and reducing risk ahead of time. Investigating a failure after the fact is the job of problem-solving methods such as 8D.
std
IV.E.5
An FMEA line has severity 8, occurrence 4 and detection 3. What is the risk priority number (RPN)?
RPN = S × O × D = 8 × 4 × 3 = 96. Adding the ratings gives 15, and S × O alone gives 32.
std
IV.E.5
After a design change, the FMEA line above (S = 8, O = 4, D = 3) is rerated with occurrence 2. Severity and detection are unchanged. What is the new RPN?
New RPN = 8 × 2 × 3 = 48. Reducing occurrence halves the RPN; severity stays the same because the effect of the failure has not changed.
std
IV.E.5
Two failure modes both have RPN = 120. Mode A has S = 10, O = 3, D = 4; mode B has S = 4, O = 10, D = 3. Which should normally be addressed first?
Mode A, because of its top severity
Mode B, because it occurs much more often than mode A
Neither, because equal RPNs mean the same level of risk
Mode B, because its detection rating is lower than A's
Equal RPNs can hide very different risks; a top severity rating usually means a safety or regulatory effect and gets priority. RPN alone should not be the only basis for ranking.
std
IV.E.6
A customer finds cracked brackets. In an 8D, what should follow forming the team and describing the problem?
Choosing the permanent corrective action
Updating standards to prevent recurrence
Recognizing the team for its quick response
Interim containment to protect the customer
D3 puts interim containment in place to protect the customer while the cause is found. Permanent corrective action comes only after the root cause is verified.
std
IV.E.6
What is the purpose of the problem description step (D2) in an 8D?
Name the department that caused the problem
State the problem in specific, measurable terms
Decide which people should serve on the team
Close the customer complaint as fast as possible
A clear, data-based problem description guides the rest of the 8D. Team selection is D1, and 8D focuses on the process, not on blame.
std
IV.E.6
In an 8D, what should happen before a permanent corrective action is implemented?
Verify that it removes the root cause without new problems
Recognize the team for finding the root cause so quickly
Remove containment so the action's effect is easier to see
Close the customer complaint so the project can wrap up
The chosen action should be verified to address the root cause and not create side effects before it is put in place. Containment stays until the permanent fix is proven.
std
IV.E.6
What is the focus of D7 in an 8D?
Containing suspect product at the customer's site
Preventing recurrence through system changes
Recognizing the team and its individual members
Writing a clear and complete problem description
D7 changes management systems, practices and procedures so this and similar problems do not happen again. Recognizing the team is D8.
std
IV.E.6
The final discipline (D8) of an 8D is mainly about:
Team recognition and closure
Writing the problem description
Verifying the root cause with data
Putting interim containment in place
D8 congratulates the team and formally closes the 8D. Containment and root cause work happen much earlier in the sequence.
std
IV.E.7

A machine stopped. Why? A fuse blew. Why? The motor overloaded. Why? A bearing was not lubricated. Why? The lube pump was worn. Why? It had no strainer, so metal chips got in. What is the best corrective action?
Lubricate the dry bearing and log the repair
Fit a strainer to keep chips out of the pump
Replace the blown fuse and restart the machine
Replace the worn lube pump with a new one
The chain ends at the missing strainer, which is the cause that, if fixed, stops the sequence. Replacing the fuse, bearing lube or pump treats symptoms, and the problem would return.
std
IV.E.7
What is a main limitation of the 5 Whys method?
It may follow one cause chain and miss others
It needs a large data set before the first why
It needs statistical software to analyze answers
It suits design problems but not process problems
Asking why down a single path can overlook other contributing causes and depends on the team's knowledge. It is a simple, data-light technique that suits many kinds of problems.
std
IV.E.7
A team's 5 Whys ends with "the operator was careless." What should the facilitator do?
Keep asking why the process allowed the error
Stop, since five questions have been asked
Accept the answer and retrain the operator
Have the operator moved to another job at once
Blaming a person usually stops short of the process cause, such as unclear methods or no error-proofing. The number five is a guide, not a rule.
std
IV.E.8
How does fault tree analysis (FTA) differ from FMEA?
FTA is used before a failure; FMEA is used after a failure occurs
FTA works down from one top event; FMEA works up from failure modes
FTA is used for attribute data; FMEA is used for variables data
FTA works up from failure modes; FMEA works down from one top event
FTA is top-down: it starts with an undesired event and finds the combinations of causes that lead to it. FMEA is bottom-up, starting with how each item can fail and tracing the effects.
std
IV.E.8
A top event occurs only if both a pump fails (probability 0.10) and its backup valve fails (0.05). The events are independent. What is the probability of the top event?
Both events must occur, so this is an AND gate: 0.10 × 0.05 = 0.005. Adding the probabilities is the OR-gate approximation, which is wrong here.
std
IV.E.8
An alarm fails if either sensor A fails (probability 0.10) or sensor B fails (0.05). The events are independent. What is the exact probability that the alarm fails?
For an OR gate, P = 1 − (1 − 0.10)(1 − 0.05) = 1 − 0.855 = 0.145. Simple addition (0.150) double-counts the case where both fail, and multiplying (0.005) is the AND gate.
std
IV.E.9
A shipment had wrong labels. The team relabels the boxes, then changes the label process so part numbers are scanned instead of typed. Which step is the corrective action?
Scanning part numbers instead of typing
Inspecting every labeled box in the warehouse
Relabeling the boxes in the affected shipment
Sending the customer a formal letter of apology
Corrective action removes the cause of a nonconformity to prevent recurrence. Relabeling and inspection fix the affected product, which is correction or containment.
std
IV.E.9
Which is a preventive action?
Reworking parts that were made with the wrong settings
Adding tests for a new material flagged by a risk review
Scrapping a material lot that failed its incoming inspection
Fixing the root cause found after a customer complaint
Preventive action addresses a potential problem before it happens. Fixing the cause of a complaint that already occurred is corrective action.
std
IV.E.9
When should a corrective or preventive action be closed?
When evidence shows the action worked
When the person who raised it agrees to close it
After a fixed number of days has passed
As soon as the action has been put in place
Closure should follow verification that the action was effective, based on evidence. Implementing an action does not show that it solved the problem.
std
IV.F.1
An inspector must use a new solvent to clean parts. Where should she look for its hazards, safe handling and first-aid measures?
The material test report
The safety data sheet (SDS)
The tank calibration record
The work instruction log
The SDS gives hazard, handling, storage, PPE and first-aid information for a chemical. A material test report covers composition and properties, not safe use.
std
IV.F.1
How does a material data sheet (MDS) differ from a safety data sheet (SDS)?
An MDS gives a material's makeup and properties; an SDS covers its hazards and safe handling
An MDS applies only to liquids, while an SDS applies only to solid materials
An MDS covers hazards and safe handling; an SDS gives the material's makeup and its properties
An MDS lists the PPE to wear, while an SDS lists the dimensional tolerances
A material data sheet describes what a material is made of and its properties, while the SDS is the hazard communication document. The two serve different purposes and apply to all forms of material.
std
IV.F.1
An inspector will check parts at a grinding station. The coolant's SDS calls for eye protection and gloves. What should he do?
Wear PPE only if he plans to touch the coolant directly
Wear the specified PPE in the area, even for a short check
Skip PPE, since inspectors do not run the grinding machine
Ask the operator to bring parts out so he can stay unprotected
PPE requirements apply to anyone exposed to the hazard, however briefly. Splash and mist exposure do not depend on who runs the machine.
std
IV.F.1
Why is PPE considered the last line of defense against a hazard?
It is required by customers rather than by law
It costs more to buy and maintain than any other type of control
It protects only the wearer and depends on correct use
It cannot be combined with engineering controls
PPE does not remove the hazard and fails if not worn or fitted properly, so elimination, substitution and engineering controls come first. It is often used alongside those controls.

IV.F.2
A drawing calls for tensile testing "per ASTM E8." What does this reference tell the inspector?
The test must follow the method in that ASTM standard
The part must come from an ISO 9001 certified supplier
The test limits are set in the customer's purchase order
The test lab must be accredited directly by NIST
ASTM publishes test methods and material standards; citing one makes its method a requirement. It says nothing about the supplier's certification or lab accreditation.
std
IV.F.2
Why do calibration certificates often state traceability to NIST?
To show that NIST has audited and certified the company's quality system
To show that NIST wrote the product specifications
To show that NIST approved the design of each gauge
To show an unbroken chain of comparisons to national standards
NIST maintains US national measurement standards, and traceability links a gauge's calibration to them through documented comparisons. NIST does not certify quality systems or approve gauge designs.
std
IV.F.2
A company wants its quality management system certified by an independent registrar. Which standard is used?
ISO 9001
ANSI/ASQ Z1.4
ISO 9000
ISO 9001 contains the certifiable QMS requirements. ISO 19011 gives guidance on auditing and ISO 9000 gives vocabulary; neither is a certification standard.
std
IV.F.2
What is ANSI's main role in US standards work?
It writes the federal product safety regulations
It inspects imported products at ports of entry
It coordinates US voluntary standards work
It maintains the national measurement standards
ANSI oversees and accredits the US voluntary consensus standards system and is the US member body of ISO. National measurement standards are NIST's role.
std
IV.F.2
QS-9000 was:
An environmental management standard that preceded ISO 14001
An aerospace quality system standard that is still required by aircraft makers
A US automotive quality system requirement, later replaced by ISO/TS 16949
A medical device regulation issued by a national health agency
QS-9000 was the quality system requirement of the major US automakers, later superseded by ISO/TS 16949 and then IATF 16949. It was neither aerospace nor environmental.
std
IV.F.2
A customer's purchase order requires 100% inspection of one dimension. The company's standard procedure samples that dimension at n = 32. What should the inspector do?
Sample 32, since that is the documented procedure
Ask the operator which of the two methods to use
Sample 32 and note the conflict in the report
Inspect 100% as the order requires

A contractual customer requirement is an authority the inspection must meet; the internal plan does not override it. Noting the conflict but not meeting the requirement still ships parts not inspected as agreed.
std
IV.F.3
Which action best shows employee empowerment?
Sending weekly defect reports from operators to managers
Posting the quality policy and objectives at every workstation in the plant
Requiring a supervisor to approve every machine adjustment
Letting operators stop the line when they find a quality problem
Empowerment gives employees the authority to act on problems in their own work. Requiring approval for every adjustment does the opposite.
std
IV.F.3
Why include line operators on an improvement team for a recurring defect?
They remove the need to collect data on the defect
They are responsible for writing the final report
They can approve spending for the chosen solution
They know how the process really runs day to day
People who do the work know its real conditions, problems and workarounds, which helps the team find causes and workable fixes. Approving spending is a sponsor or manager role.
std
IV.F.3
What is the main role of a team facilitator?
To guide how the team works together
To carry out the technical analysis for the team members
To make the final decisions on behalf of the whole team
To record the minutes and actions of each team meeting
A facilitator manages how the team works together, keeping discussion focused and balanced. Recording minutes is the scribe's job, and decisions belong to the team.
std
IV.F.3
A team's meetings start late and one member dominates them. What would help most at the next meeting?
Remove the dominant member from the team without discussion
Agree ground rules on start times and how everyone is heard
Ask the sponsor to attend and run every meeting from now on
Cancel meetings and move all team work to email threads
Ground rules set agreed norms for behavior, such as punctuality and equal participation. Removing a member or abandoning meetings avoids the issue rather than fixing it.
std
IV.F.3
Which content belongs in a team charter?
The minutes from every team meeting held so far
The final solution and its estimated cost
The verified root cause of the problem
The problem, goal, scope, members and timeline
A charter is written at the start to set the team's purpose, boundaries, membership and timing. The root cause and solution are outputs of the project, not inputs.
std
IV.F.3
A new team is polite and unsure of its purpose, and members look to the leader for direction. Which stage of team development is this?
Forming
Norming
Adjourning
Storming
Forming is the first stage, marked by politeness, uncertainty and dependence on the leader. Storming follows when members begin to push back and disagree.
std
IV.F.3
Team members argue about roles and approach, and some challenge the leader. Which stage of team development is this?
Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
Storming is marked by conflict over roles, goals and methods. Norming follows once members settle on how they will work together.
std
IV.F.3
Members have accepted their roles, agreed on how to work and conflict has eased. Which stage of team development is this?
Storming
Forming
Norming
Performing
Norming is when the team settles its working rules and relationships. Performing comes after, when the team works smoothly and independently toward its goal.
std
IV.F.3
A team now works independently, solves its own problems and makes steady progress toward its goal. Which stage is this?
Storming
Performing
Adjourning
Norming
Performing is the stage of high productivity and self-direction. Norming is the earlier stage when the team was still settling how to work.
std
IV.F.3
A team finishes its project, hands the process back to its owner, celebrates and disbands. Which stage is this?
Norming
Performing
Adjourning
Forming
Adjourning is the final stage, when the team wraps up and members move on. Performing is the productive stage that came before.
std
IV.F.4
An inspector finds that the printed work instruction at a station is revision C, but the controlled system shows revision D. What should she do?
Mark revision C as current so it matches the station copy
Use revision C until the shift ends, then report the problem
Keep using revision C, since printed copies are easier to read
Stop using revision C and get revision D before going on
Work must be done to the current approved revision, and an obsolete copy at the point of use should be removed. Continuing with it, even briefly, risks product made to old requirements.
std
IV.F.4
When is a first article inspection typically required?
For every production lot shipped, whether or not anything has changed
After every calibration of the gauges used on the part
Only after a customer complaint about the part is received
For a new part, or after a change in design, process or tooling
A first article inspection verifies that a new or changed setup can produce a part that meets every drawing requirement. Unchanged lots are covered by routine inspection, not repeated FAIs.
std
IV.F.4
An initial sample inspection report (ISIR) is used to:
Record daily SPC data for a process that has already been shown to be stable
Document the investigation of a customer complaint about a part
Show that samples from production tooling meet all drawing requirements
Report the results of an internal audit of the quality system
An ISIR records full measurement and test results on initial samples made with production tooling and processes. Daily SPC and complaint investigations are separate records.

IV.F.4
What is the main purpose of the production part approval process (PPAP)?
To replace ongoing inspection once the parts have been approved
To show the supplier understands all requirements and can make good parts at rate
To agree the price the customer will pay for production parts
To certify the supplier's quality management system against the ISO 9001 standard

PPAP gives evidence that the supplier understands the design and specification requirements and that its production process can consistently meet them at the quoted rate. It does not replace ongoing controls.
std
IV.F.4
Under ISO 9001:2015, which is documented information that must be retained as a record, rather than maintained?
The quality policy statement
Calibration results
The documented scope of the QMS
The quality objectives for the year
Evidence of calibration is retained documented information, a record of results. The policy, scope and objectives are maintained documented information that states intent and is updated.

IV.F.4
Which document typically tells an operator, step by step, how to do one task at a workstation?
Blank inspection form
Work instruction
Departmental procedure
Quality policy statement
Work instructions give detailed steps for a specific task. A procedure describes a process more broadly, such as who does what and when across functions.

IV.F.4
Once an inspection form has been filled in and signed, it is best described as:
A procedure describing how a process works
A record giving evidence of what was done
A work instruction for the inspection task
A policy stating management's intentions
A completed form becomes a record, which is evidence of activities and results. Policies, procedures and work instructions state how things should be done.

IV.F.4
An inspector writes a wrong reading on a paper inspection form. What is the correct way to fix it?
Start a fresh copy of the form and throw away the original one with the error
Write over the old number so that it reads as the right value
Draw one line through it, write the right value, then initial and date
Cover it with correction fluid and write the right value on top
Good practice keeps the original entry legible and shows who changed it and when. Correction fluid, overwriting or discarding the form destroys the evidence.

IV.F.4
A field on an inspection form does not apply to the current lot. What is good documentation practice?
Leave the field blank, since it does not apply to the current lot
Enter N/A and initial it, so the field is clearly not missed
Cross the field off the form by hand for future use
Copy in the value recorded for the previous lot
Filling every field, even with N/A, shows the field was considered and not overlooked. Blank fields leave the record incomplete and open to later entries.

IV.F.4
What is the main purpose of document control?
Make sure approved, current versions are used and obsolete ones are not
Keep every past revision of each document at each workstation for reference
Make sure documents stay unchanged after their first release
Limit who is allowed to read any of the quality documents

Document control ensures documents are approved, available at the point of use in their current revision, and that obsolete versions are kept out of use. Documents are expected to be revised through a controlled change process.
